entries.943e1f84dc704b2be397259deeda34c1766b7781: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv121"/><title type="x-ms">First Timothy</title> <div sID="gen32352" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32353" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Hitherto</hi> Paul's epistles were directed to churches; now follow some to particular persons: two to Timothy, one to Titus, and another to Philemon—all three ministers. Timothy and Titus were evangelists, an inferior order to the apostles, as appears by <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Some prophets, some apostles, some evangelists.</hi> Their commission and work was much the same with that of the apostles, to plant churches, and water the churches that were planted; and accordingly they were itinerants, as we find Timothy was. Timothy was first converted by Paul, and therefore he calls him his <hi type="italic">own son in the faith:</hi> we read of his conversion, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.3">Acts xvi. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen32353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32354" type="x-p"/> The scope of these two epistles is to direct Timothy how to discharge his duty as an evangelist at Ephesus, where he now was, and where Paul ordered him for some time to reside, to perfect the good work which he had begun there. As for the ordinary pastoral charge of that church, he had very solemnly committed it to the presbytery, as appears from <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Acts xx. 28</reference>, where he charges the presbyters <hi type="italic">to feed the flock of God, which he had purchased with his own blood.</hi> <div eID="gen32354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32355" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32356" type="x-p"/> After the inscription (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1-1Tim.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) we have, I. The charge given to Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3-1Tim.1.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. II. The true end of the law (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5-1Tim.1.11">ver. 5-11</reference>), where he shows that it is entirely agreeable to the gospel. III. He mentions his own call to be an apostle, for which he expresses his thankfulness, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12-1Tim.1.16">ver. 12-16</reference>. IV. His doxology, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">ver. 17</reference>. V. A renewal of the charge to Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">ver. 18</reference>. And of Hymenæus and Alexander, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19-1Tim.1.20">ver. 19, 20</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv121"/> <div eID="gen32356" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32355" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Inscription and Apostolic Benediction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32357" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> our hope; <hi type="super">2</hi> Unto Timothy, <hi type="italic">my</hi> own son in the faith: Grace, mercy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> peace, from God our Father and Jesus Christ our Lord. <hi type="super">3</hi> As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia, that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine, <hi type="super">4</hi> Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: <hi type="italic">so do.</hi> <div eID="gen32357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32358" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The inscription of the epistle, from whom it is sent: <hi type="italic">Paul an apostle of Jesus Christ,</hi> constituted an apostle <hi type="italic">by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> His credentials were unquestionable. He had not only a commission, but a commandment, not only from God our Saviour, but from Jesus Christ: he was a preacher of the gospel of Christ, and a minister of the kingdom of Christ. Observe, God is our Saviour.—<hi type="italic">Jesus Christ, who is our hope.</hi> Observe, Jesus Christ is a Christian's hope; our hope is in him, all our hope of eternal life is built upon him; Christ is in us the hope of glory, <reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col. i. 27</reference>. He calls Timothy his own son, because he had been an instrument of his conversion, and because he had been a son that served him, served with him in the gospel, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.22">Phil. ii. 22</reference>. Timothy had not been wanting in the duty of a son to Paul, and Paul was not wanting in the care and tenderness of a father to him. <div eID="gen32358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32359" type="x-p"/> II. The benediction is, <hi type="italic">grace, mercy, and peace, from God our Father.</hi> Some have observed that whereas in all the epistles to the churches the apostolical benediction is <hi type="italic">grace and peace,</hi> in these two epistles to Timothy and that to Titus it is <hi type="italic">grace, mercy, and peace:</hi> as if ministers had more need of God's mercy than other men. Ministers need more grace than others, to discharge their duty faithfully; and they need more mercy than others, to pardon what is amiss in them: and if Timothy, so eminent a minister, must be indebted to the mercy of God, and needed the increase and continuance of it, how much more do we ministers, in these times, who have so little of his excellent spirit! <div eID="gen32359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32360" type="x-p"/> III. Paul tells Timothy what was the end of his appointing him to this office: <hi type="italic">I besought thee to abide at Ephesus.</hi> Timothy had a mind to go with Paul, was loth to go from under his wing, but Paul would have it so; it was necessary for the public service: <hi type="italic">I besought thee,</hi> says he. Though he might assume an authority to command him, yet for love's sake he chose rather to beseech him. Now his business was to take care to fix both the ministers and the people of that church: <hi type="italic">Charge them that they teach no other doctrine</hi> than what they have received, that they do not add to the Christian doctrine, under pretence of improving it or making up the defects of it, that they do no alter it, but cleave to it as it was delivered to them. Observe, 1. Ministers must not only be charged to preach the true doctrine of the gospel, but charged to preach no other doctrine. <hi type="italic">If an angel from heaven preach any other doctrine, let him be anathema,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8">Gal. i. 8</reference>. 2. In the times of the apostles there were attempts made to corrupt Christianity (<hi type="italic">we are not as many, who corrupt the word,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2 Cor. ii. 17</reference>), otherwise this charge to Timothy might have been spared. 3. He must not only see to it that he did not preach any other doctrine, but he must charge others that they might not add any thing of their own to the gospel, or take any thing from it, but that they preach it pure and uncorrupt. He must also take care to prevent their regarding <hi type="italic">fables, and endless genealogies,</hi> and strifes of words. This is often repeated in these two epistles (as <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">vi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">2 Tim. ii. 23</reference>), as well as in the epistle to Titus. As among the Jews there were some who brought Judaism into Christianity; so among the Gentiles there were some who brought paganism into Christianity. "Take heed of these," says he, "watch against them, or they will be the corrupting and ruining of religion among you, for <hi type="italic">they minister questions rather than edifying.</hi>" That which ministers questions is not for edifying; that which gives occasion for doubtful disputes pulls down the church rather than builds it up. And I think, by a parity of reason, every thing else that ministers questions rather than godly edifying should be disclaimed and disregarded by us, such as an uninterrupted succession in the ministry from the apostles down to these times, the absolute necessity of episcopal ordination, and of the intention of the minister to the efficacy and validity of the sacraments he ministers. These are as bad as Jewish fables and endless genealogies, for they involve us in inextricable difficulties, and tend only to shake the foundations of a Christian's hope and to fill his mind with perplexing doubts and fears. Godly edifying is the end ministers should aim at in all their discourses, that Christians may be improving in godliness and growing up to a greater likeness to the blessed God. Observe, further, Godly edifying must be in faith: the gospel is the foundation on which we build; it is by faith that we come to God at first (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>), and it must be in the same way, and by the same principle of faith, that we must be edified. Again, Ministers should avoid, as much as may be, what will occasion disputes; and would do well to insist on the great and practical points of religion, about which there can be no disputes; for even disputes about great and necessary truths draw off the mind from the main design of Christianity, and eat out the vitals of religion, which consist in practice and obedience as well as in faith, that we may not hold the truth in unrighteousness, but may keep the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.
entries.a6ad92ee272b1598d9ba3d3088e7808d976dcfd2: <div eID="gen32360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Timothy Reminded of His Charge. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32361" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> a good conscience, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> faith unfeigned: <hi type="super">6</hi> From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling; <hi type="super">7</hi> Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm. <hi type="super">8</hi> But we know that the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> good, if a man use it lawfully; <hi type="super">9</hi> Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, <hi type="super">10</hi> For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine; <hi type="super">11</hi> According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust. <div eID="gen32361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32362" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle instructs Timothy how to guard against the judaizing teachers, or others who mingled fables and endless genealogies with the gospel. He shows the use of the law, and the glory of the gospel. <div eID="gen32362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32363" type="x-p"/> I. He shows the end and uses of the law: it is intended to promote love, <hi type="italic">for love is the fulfilling of the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.10">Rom. xiii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen32363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32364" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The end of the commandment is charity,</hi> or love, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.8">Rom. xiii. 8</reference>. The main scope and drift of the divine law are to engage us to the love of God and one another; and whatever tends to weaken either our love to God or love to the brethren tends to defeat the end of the commandment: and surely the gospel, which obliges us to love our enemies, to do good to those who hate us (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Matt. v. 44</reference>) does not design to lay aside or supersede a commandment the end whereof is love; so far from it that, on the other hand, we are told that though we had all advantages and wanted charity, we are but as sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1">1 Cor. xiii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you love one another,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.35">John xiii. 35</reference>. Those therefore who boasted of their knowledge of the law, but used it only as a colour for the disturbance that they gave to the preaching of the gospel (under pretence of zeal for the law, dividing the church and distracting it), defeated that which was the very end of the commandment, and that is love, love <hi type="italic">out of a pure heart,</hi> a heart purified by faith, purified from corrupt affections. In order to the keeping up of holy love our hearts must be cleansed from all sinful love; our love must arise <hi type="italic">out of a good conscience,</hi> kept without offence. Those answer the end of the commandment who are careful to keep a good conscience, from a real belief of the truth of the word of God which enjoins it, here called a <hi type="italic">faith unfeigned.</hi> Here we have the concomitants of that excellency grace charity; they are three:—(1.) A pure heart; there it must be seated, and thence it must take its rise. (2.) A good conscience, in which we must exercise ourselves daily, that we may not only get it, but that we may keep it, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Acts xxiv. 16</reference>. (3.) Faith unfeigned must also accompany it, for it is love without dissimulation: the faith that works by it must be of the like nature, genuine and sincere. Now some who set up for teachers of the law swerved from the very end of the commandment: they set up for disputers, but their disputes proved vain jangling; they set up for teachers, but they pretended to teach others what they themselves did not understand. If the church be corrupted by such teachers, we must not think it strange, for we see from the beginning it was so. Observe, [1.] When persons, especially ministers, swerve from the great law of charity—the end of the commandment, they will turn aside to vain jangling; when a man misses his end and scope, it is no wonder that every step he takes is out of the way. [2.] Jangling, especially in religion, is vain; it is unprofitable and useless as to all that is good, and it is very pernicious and hurtful: and yet many people's religion consists of little else but vain jangling. [3.] Those who deal much in vain jangling are fond and ambitious to be teachers of others; they desire (that is, they affect) the office of teaching. [4.] It is too common for men to intrude into the office of the ministry when they are very ignorant of those things about which they are ton speak: they understand neither what they say nor whereof they affirm; and by such learned ignorance, no doubt, they edify their hearers very much! <div eID="gen32364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32365" type="x-p"/> 2. The use of the law (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">The law is good, if a man use it lawfully.</hi> The Jews used it unlawfully, as an engine to divide the church, a cover to the malicious opposition they made to the gospel of Christ; they set it up for justification, and so used it unlawfully. We must not therefore think to set it aside, but use it lawfully, for the restraint of sin. The abuse which some have made of the law does not take away the use of it; but, when a divine appointment has been abused, call it back to its right use and take away the abuses, for the law is still very useful as a rule of life; though we are not under it as under a covenant of works, yet it is good to teach us what is sin and what is duty. It is not made for a righteous man, that is, it is not made for those who observe it; for, if we could keep the law, righteousness would be by the law (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">Gal. iii. 21</reference>): but it is made for wicked persons, to restrain them, to check them, and to put a stop to vice and profaneness. It is the grace of God that changes men's hearts; but the terrors of the law may be of use to tie their hands and restrain their tongues. A righteous man does not want those restraints which are necessary for the wicked; or at least the law is not made primarily and principally for the righteous, but for sinners of all sorts, whether in a greater or less measure, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9-1Tim.1.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. In this black roll of sinners, he particularly mentions breaches of the second table, duties which we owe to our neighbour; against the fifth and sixth commandments, <hi type="italic">murderers of fathers and mothers, and manslayers;</hi> against the seventh, <hi type="italic">whoremongers, and those that defile themselves with mankind;</hi> against the eighth, <hi type="italic">men-stealers;</hi> against the ninth, <hi type="italic">liars and perjured persons;</hi> and then he closes his account with this, <hi type="italic">and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine.</hi> Some understand this as an institution of a power in the civil magistrate to make laws against such notorious sinners as are specified, and to see those laws put in execution. <div eID="gen32365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32366" type="x-p"/> II. He shows the glory and grace of the gospel. Paul's epithets are expressive and significant; and frequently every one is a sentence: as here (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God.</hi> Let us learn hence, 1. To call God blessed God, infinitely happy in the enjoyment of himself and his own perfections. 2. To call the gospel the glorious gospel, for so it is: much of the glory of God appears in the works of creation and providence, but much more in the gospel, where it shines in the face of Jesus Christ. Paul reckoned it a great honour put upon him, and a great favour done him, that this glorious gospel was committed to his trust; that is, the preaching of it, for the framing of it is not committed to any man or company of men in the world. The settling of the terms of salvation in the gospel of Christ is God's own work; but the publishing of it to the world is committed to the apostles and ministers. Note here, (1.) The ministry is a trust, for the gospel was committed unto this apostle; it is an office of trust as well as of power, and the former more than the latter; for this reason ministers are called stewards, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">1 Cor. iv. 1</reference>. (2.) It is a glorious trust, because the gospel committed to them is a glorious gospel; it is a trust of very great importance. God's glory is very much concerned in it. Lord, what a trust is committed to us! How much grace do we want, to be found faithful in this great trust!
entries.1d42b2adda038c02f8d28b8e96380b0e87b71d22: <div eID="gen32366" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Perverters Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32367" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry; <hi type="super">13</hi> Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did <hi type="italic">it</hi> ignorantly in unbelief. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the grace of our Lord was exceeding abundant with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. 15 This <hi type="italic">is</hi> a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. <hi type="super">16</hi> Howbeit for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show forth all longsuffering, for a pattern to them which should hereafter believe on him to life everlasting. <hi type="super">17</hi> Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, <hi type="italic">be</hi> honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen. <div eID="gen32367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32368" type="x-p"/> Here the apostle, I. Returns thanks to Jesus Christ for putting him into the ministry. Observe, 1. It is Christ's work to put men into the ministry, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.16-Acts.26.17">Acts xxvi. 16, 17</reference>. God condemned the false prophets among the Jews in these words, <hi type="italic">I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: I have not spoken to them, yet they prophesied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jer. xxiii. 21</reference>. Ministers, properly speaking, cannot make themselves ministers; for it is Christ's work, as king and head, prophet and teacher, of his church. 2. Those whom he puts into the ministry he fits for it; whom he calls he qualifies. Those ministers who are no way fit for their work, nor have ability for it, are not of Christ's putting into the ministry, though there are different qualifications as to gifts and graces. 3. Christ gives not only ability, but fidelity, to those whom he puts into the ministry: He <hi type="italic">counted me faithful;</hi> and none are counted faithful but those whom he makes so. Christ's ministers are trusty servants, and they ought to be so, having so great a trust committed to them. 4. A call to the ministry is a great favour, for which those who are so called ought to give thanks to Jesus Christ: <hi type="italic">I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath put me into the ministry.</hi> <div eID="gen32368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32369" type="x-p"/> II. The more to magnify the grace of Christ in putting him into the ministry, he gives an account of his conversion. <div eID="gen32369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32370" type="x-p"/> 1. What he was before his conversion: <hi type="italic">A blasphemer, a persecutor, and injurious.</hi> Saul breathed out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.1">Acts ix. 1</reference>. He made havoc of the church, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.3">Acts viii. 3</reference>. He was a blasphemer of God, a persecutor of the saints, and injurious to both. Frequently those who are designed for great and eminent services are left to themselves before their conversion, to fall into great wickedness, that the mercy of God may be the more glorified in their remission, and the grace of God in their regeneration. The greatness of sin is no bar to our acceptance with God, no, nor to our being employed for him, if it be truly repented of. Observe here, (1.) Blasphemy, persecution, and injuriousness, are very great and heinous sins, and those who are guilty of them are sinners before God exceedingly. To blaspheme God is immediately and directly to strike at God; to persecute his people is to endeavour to wound him through their sides; and to be injurious is to be like Ishmael, whose hand was against every one, and every one was against him; for such invade God's prerogative, and encroach upon the liberties of their fellow-creatures. (2.) True penitents, to serve a good purpose, will not be backward to own their former condition before they were brought home to God: this good apostle often confessed what his former life had been, as <reference osisRef="Acts.22.4">Acts xxii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.10-Acts.26.11">xxvi. 10, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen32370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32371" type="x-p"/> 2. The great favour of God to him: <hi type="italic">But I obtained mercy.</hi> This was a blessed <hi type="italic">but</hi> indeed, a great favour, that so notorious a rebel should find mercy with his prince. <div eID="gen32371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32372" type="x-p"/> (1.) If Paul had persecuted the Christians wilfully, knowing them to be the people of God, for aught I know he had been guilty of the unpardonable sin; but, because he did it ignorantly and in unbelief, he obtained mercy. Note, [1.] What we do ignorantly is a less crime than what we do knowingly; yet a sin of ignorance is a sin, for he that knew not his Master's will, but did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.48">Luke xii. 48</reference>. Ignorance in some cases will extenuate a crime, though it do not take it away. [2.] Unbelief is at the bottom of what sinners do ignorantly; they do not believe God's threatenings, otherwise they could not do as they do. [3.] For these reasons Paul obtained mercy: <hi type="italic">But I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly, in unbelief.</hi> [4.] Here was mercy for a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious person: "<hi type="italic">But I obtained mercy,</hi> I a blasphemer," &c. <div eID="gen32372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32373" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here he takes notice of the abundant grace of Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.14">v. 14</reference>. The conversion and salvation of great sinners are owing to the grace of Christ, his exceedingly abundant grace, even that grace of Christ which appears in his glorious gospel (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is a faithful saying,</hi> &c. Here we have the sum of the whole gospel, <hi type="italic">that Jesus Christ came into the world.</hi> The Son of God took upon him our nature, was made flesh, and dwelt among us, <reference osisRef="John.1.14">John i. 14</reference>. He came into the world, <hi type="italic">not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Matt. ix. 13</reference>. His errand into the world was to seek and find, and so save, <hi type="italic">those that were lost,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.10">Luke xix. 10</reference>. The ratification of this is <hi type="italic">that it is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation.</hi> It is good news, worthy of all acceptation; and yet not too good to be true, for it is a faithful saying. It is a faithful saying, and therefore worthy to be embraced in the arms of faith: it is worthy of all acceptation, and therefore to be received with holy love, which refers to the <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.14">foregoing verse</reference>, where the grace of Christ is said to abound in faith and love. In the close of <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">the verse</reference> Paul applies it to himself: <hi type="italic">Of whom I am chief.</hi> Paul was a sinner of the first rank; so he acknowledges himself to have been, for he breathed out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, &c., <reference osisRef="Acts.9.1-Acts.9.2">Acts ix. 1, 2</reference>. Persecutors are some of the worst of sinners: such a one Paul had been. Or, <hi type="italic">of whom I am chief,</hi> that is, of pardoned sinners I am chief. It is an expression of his great humility; he that elsewhere calls himself the <hi type="italic">least of all saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Eph. iii. 8</reference>) here calls himself the chief of sinners. Observe, [1.] Christ Jesus has come into the world; the prophecies concerning his coming are now fulfilled. [2.] He came to save sinners; he came to save those who could not save and help themselves. [3.] Blasphemers and persecutors are the chief of sinners, so Paul reckoned them. [4.] The chief of sinners may become the chief of saints; so this apostle was, for he was not a whit behind the very chief apostles (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5">2 Cor. xi. 5</reference>), for Christ came to save the chief of sinners. [5.] This is a very great truth, it is a faithful saying; these are true and faithful words, which may be depended on. [6.] It deserves to be received, to be believed by us all, for our comfort and encouragement. <div eID="gen32373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32374" type="x-p"/> (3.) The mercy which Paul found with God, notwithstanding his great wickedness before his conversion, he speaks of, <div eID="gen32374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32375" type="x-p"/> [1.] For the encouragement of others to repent and believe (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">For this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show forth all long-suffering, for a pattern to those who should hereafter believe.</hi> It was an instance of the long-suffering of Christ that he would bear so much with one who had been so very provoking; and it was designed for a pattern to all others, that the greatest sinners might not despair of mercy with God. Note here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Our apostle was one of the first great sinners converted to Christianity. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He was converted, and obtained mercy, for the sake of others as well as of himself; he was a pattern to others. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The Lord Jesus Christ shows great long-suffering in the conversion of great sinners. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> Those who obtain mercy believe on the Lord Jesus Christ; for without faith it is impossible to please God, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> Those who believe on Christ believe on him to life everlasting; they believe to the saving of the soul, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.39">Heb. x. 39</reference>. <div eID="gen32375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32376" type="x-p"/> [2.] He mentions it to the glory of God having spoken of the mercy he had found with God, he could not go on with his letter without inserting a thankful acknowledgment of God's goodness to him: <hi type="italic">Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.</hi> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That grace which we have the comfort of God must have the glory of. Those who are sensible of their obligations to the mercy and grace of God will have their hearts enlarged in his praise. Here is praise ascribed to him, as <hi type="italic">the King eternal, immortal, invisible. Secondly,</hi> When we have found God good we must not forget to pronounce him great; and his kind thoughts of us must not at all abate our high thoughts of him, but rather increase them. God had taken particular cognizance of Paul, and shown him mercy, and taken him into communion with himself, and yet he calls him the King eternal, &c. God's gracious dealings with us should fill us with admiration of his glorious attributes. He is eternal, without beginning of days, or end of life, or change of time. He is the Ancient of days, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Dan. vii. 9</reference>. He is immortal, and the original of immortality; he only has immortality (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1 Tim. vi. 16</reference>), for he cannot die. He is invisible, for he cannot be seen with mortal eyes, dwelling in the light to which no man can approach, whom no man hath seen nor can see, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1 Tim. vi. 16</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">the only wise God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.25">Jude 25</reference>); he only is infinitely wise, and the fountain of all wisdom. "<hi type="italic">To him be glory for ever and ever,</hi>" or, "Let me be for ever employed in giving honour and glory to him, as the thousands of thousands do," <reference osisRef="Rev.5.12-Rev.5.13">Rev. v. 12, 13</reference>.
entries.fa2886af4a0c399e79b4ea4465d4874d83d3d4db: <div eID="gen32376" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Charge to Timothy. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32377" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare; <hi type="super">19</hi> Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck: <hi type="super">20</hi> Of whom is Hymenæus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme. <div eID="gen32377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32378" type="x-p"/> Here is the charge he gives to Timothy to proceed in his work with resolution, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">v. 18</reference>. Observe here, The gospel is a charge committed to the ministers of it; it is committed to their trust, to see that it be duly applied according to the intent and meaning of it, and the design of its great Author. It seems, there had been prophecies before concerning Timothy, that he should be taken into the ministry, and should prove eminent in the work of the ministry; this encouraged Paul to commit this charge to him. Observe, 1. The ministry is a warfare, it is a good warfare against sin and Satan: and under the banner of the Lord Jesus, who is the Captain of our salvation (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>), and in his cause, and against his enemies, ministers are in a particular manner engaged. 2. Ministers must war this good warfare, must execute their office diligently and courageously, notwithstanding oppositions and discouragements. 3. The prophecies which went before concerning Timothy are here mentioned as a motive to stir him up to a vigorous and conscientious discharge of his duty; so the good hopes that others have entertained concerning us should excite us to our duty: <hi type="italic">That thou by them mightest war a good warfare.</hi> 4. We must hold both faith and a good conscience: <hi type="italic">Holding faith and a good conscience,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">v. 19</reference>. Those that put away a good conscience will soon make shipwreck of faith. Let us live up to the directions of a renewed enlightened conscience, and keep conscience void of offence (<reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Acts xxiv. 16</reference>), a conscience not debauched by any vice or sin, and this will be a means of preserving us sound in the faith; we must look to the one as well a the other, for the mystery of the faith must be held in a pure conscience, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.9">ch. iii. 9</reference>. As for those who had made shipwreck of the faith, he specifies two, <hi type="italic">Hymeneus and Alexander,</hi> who had made a profession of the Christian religion, but had quitted that profession; and Paul had delivered them to Satan, had declared them to belong to the kingdom of Satan, and, as some think, had, by an extraordinary power, delivered them to be terrified or tormented by Satan, <hi type="italic">that they might learn not to blaspheme</hi> not to contradict or revile the doctrine of Christ and the good ways of the Lord. Observe, The primary design of the highest censure in the primitive church was to prevent further sin and to reclaim the sinner. In this case it was for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">1 Cor. v. 5</reference>. Observe, (1.) Those who love the service and work of Satan are justly delivered over to the power of Satan: <hi type="italic">Whom I have delivered over to Satan.</hi> (2.) God can, if he please, work by contraries: Hymeneus and Alexander are delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme, when one would rather think they would learn of Satan to blaspheme the more. (3.) Those who have put away a good conscience, and made shipwreck of faith, will not stick at any thing, blasphemy not excepted. (4.) Therefore let us hold faith and a good conscience, if we would keep clear of blasphemy; for, if we once let go our hold of these, we do not know where we shall stop.  <chapter eID="1Tim.1"/> <div eID="gen32378" type="x-p"/>

entries.fb60d4128a29c269e93bfd7e53de7bcad2cb5f12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18056"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen37040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Genuineness.--</hi>The ancient Church never doubted of their being canonical and written by Paul. They are in the Peschito Syriac version of the second century. Muratori's Fragment on the Canon of Scripture, at the close of the second century, acknowledges them as such. Irenæus [Against Heresies, 1; 3.3.3; 4.16.3; 2.14.8; 3.11.1; 1.16.3], quotes <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.9-2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.10">Tit 3:10</reference>. Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 2, p. 457; 3, pp. 534, 536; 1, p. 350], quotes <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">1Ti 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">20</reference>; Second Timothy, as to deaconesses; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>. Tertullian [The Prescription against Heretics, 25; 6], quotes <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.14">2Ti 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">6:13</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">2Ti 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.10">Tit 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.11">11</reference>. Eusebius includes the three in the "universally acknowledged" Scriptures. Also Theophilus of Antioch [To Autolychus, 3.14], quotes <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.1">Tit 3:1</reference>, and Caius (in Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 6.20]) recognizes their authenticity. Clement of Rome, in the end of the first century, in his first Epistle to the Corinthians [29], quotes <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Ti 2:8</reference>. Ignatius, in the beginning of the second century, in Epistle to Polycarp, [6], alludes to <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">2Ti 2:4</reference>. Polycarp, in the beginning of the second century [Epistle to the Philippians, 4], alludes to <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.4">2Ti 2:4</reference>; and in the ninth chapter to <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>. Hegisippus, in the end of the second century, in Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 3.32], alludes to <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">20</reference>. Athenagoras, in the end of the second century, alludes to <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>. Justin Martyr, in the middle of the second century [Dialogue with Trypho, 47], alludes to <reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>. The Gnostic Marcion alone rejected these Epistles.<div eID="gen37040" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37039" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37041" type="x-p"/> The HERESIES OPPOSED in them form the transition stage from Judaism, in its ascetic form, to Gnosticism, as subsequently developed. The references to Judaism and legalism are clear (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3">4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.10">Tit 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>). Traces of beginning Gnosticism are also unequivocal (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>). The Gnostic theory of a twofold principle from the beginning, evil as well as good, appears in germ in <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, &c. In <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference> the term Gnosis ("science") itself occurs. Another Gnostic error, namely, that "the resurrection is past," is alluded to in <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>, 18. The Judaism herein opposed is not that of the earlier Epistles, which upheld the law and tried to join it with faith in Christ for justification. It first passed into that phase of it which appears in the Epistle to the Colossians, whereby will-worship and angel-worship were superadded to Judaizing opinions. Then a further stage of the same evil appears in the Epistle to the Philippians (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.2">Php 3:2</reference>, 18, 19), whereby immoral practice accompanied false doctrine as to the resurrection (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>, with <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.12">1Co 15:12</reference>, 32, 33). This descent from legality to superstition, and from superstition to godlessness, appears more matured in the references to it in these Pastoral Epistles. The false teachers now know not the true use of the law (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>), and further, have put away good conscience as well as the faith (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">1Ti 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>); speak lies in hypocrisy, are corrupt in mind, and regard godliness as a means of earthly gain (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.5">1Ti 6:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>); overthrow the faith by heresies eating as a canker, saying the resurrection is past (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>, 18), leading captive silly women, ever learning yet never knowing the truth, reprobate as Jannes and Jambres (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.6">2Ti 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.8">8</reference>), defiled, unbelieving, professing to know God, but in works denying Him, abominable, disobedient, reprobate (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>). This description accords with that in the Catholic Epistles of St. John and St. Peter, and, in the Epistle to the Hebrews. This fact proves the later date of these Pastoral Epistles as compared with Paul's earlier Epistles. The Judaism reprobated herein is not that of an earlier date, so scrupulous as to the law; it was now tending to immortality of practice. On the other hand, the Gnosticism opposed in these Epistles is not the anti-Judaic Gnosticism of a later date, which arose as a consequence of the overthrow of Judaism by the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, but it was the intermediate phase between Judaism and Gnosticism, in which the Oriental and Greek elements of the latter were in a kind of amalgam with Judaism, just prior to the overthrow of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen37041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37042" type="x-p"/> The DIRECTIONS AS TO CHURCH GOVERNORS and ministers, "bishop-elders, and deacons," are such as were natural for the apostle, in prospect of his own approaching removal, to give to Timothy, the president of the Church at Ephesus, and to Titus, holding the same office in Crete, for securing the due administration of the Church when he should be no more, and at a time when heresies were rapidly springing up. Compare his similar anxiety in his address to the Ephesian elders (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.21-Acts.20.30">Ac 20:21-30</reference>). The Presbyterate (elders; priest is a contraction from presbyter) and Diaconate had existed from the earliest times in the Church (<reference osisRef="Acts.6.3">Ac 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.11.30">11:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.23">14:23</reference>). Timothy and Titus, as superintendents or overseers (so bishop subsequently meant), were to exercise the same power in ordaining elders at Ephesus which the apostle had exercised in his general supervision of all the Gentile churches.<div eID="gen37042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37043" type="x-p"/> The PECULIARITIES OF MODES OF THOUGHT AND EXPRESSION, are such as the difference of subject and circumstances of those addressed and those spoken of in these Epistles, as compared with the other Epistles, would lead us to expect. Some of these peculiar phrases occur also in Galatians, in which, as in the Pastoral Epistles, he, with his characteristic fervor, attacks the false teachers. Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>, "gave Himself for us," with <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">1Ti 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">2Ti 4:18</reference>, "for ever and ever," with <reference osisRef="Gal.1.5">Ga 1:5</reference>: "before God," <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Ti 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Gal.1.20">Ga 1:20</reference>: "a pillar," <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Ga 2:9</reference>: "mediator," <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Gal.3.20">Ga 3:20</reference>: "in due season," <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Ti 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">Ga 6:9</reference>.<div eID="gen37043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Time and place of writing.--</hi>The First Epistle to Timothy was written not long after Paul had left Ephesus for Macedon (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>). Now, as Timothy was in Macedon with Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>) on the occasion of Paul's having passed from Ephesus into that country, as recorded, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">20:1</reference>, whereas the First Epistle to Timothy contemplates a longer stay of Timothy in Ephesus, Mosheim supposes that Paul was nine months of the "three years" stay mostly at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.31">Ac 20:31</reference>) in Macedonia, and elsewhere (perhaps Crete), (the mention of only "three months" and "two years," <reference osisRef="Acts.19.8">Ac 19:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.10">10</reference>, favors this, the remaining nine months being spent elsewhere); and that during these nine months Timothy, in Paul's absence, superintended the Church of Ephesus. It is not likely that Ephesus and the neighboring churches should have been left long without church officers and church organization, rules respecting which are giver in this Epistle. Moreover, Timothy was still "a youth" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>), which he could hardly be called after Paul's first imprisonment, when he must have been at least thirty-four years of age. Lastly, in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.25">Ac 20:25</reference>, Paul asserts his knowledge that the Ephesians should not all see his face again, so that <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference> will thus refer to his sojourn at Ephesus, recorded in <reference osisRef="Acts.19.10">Ac 19:10</reference>, whence he passed into Macedonia. But the difficulty is to account for the false teachers having sprung up almost immediately (according to this theory) after the foundation of the Church. However, his visit recorded in <reference osisRef="Acts.19.1-Acts.19.41">Ac 19:1-41</reference> was not his first visit. The beginning of the Church at Ephesus was probably made at his visit a year before (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.19-Acts.18.21">Ac 18:19-21</reference>). Apollos, Aquila and Priscilla, carried on the work (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.24-Acts.18.26">Ac 18:24-26</reference>). Thus, as to the sudden growth of false teachers, there was time enough for their springing up, especially considering that the first converts at Ephesus were under Apollos' imperfect Christian teachings at first, imbued as he was likely to be with the tenets of Philo of Alexandria, Apollos' native town, combined with John the Baptist's Old Testament teachings (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.24-Acts.18.26">Ac 18:24-26</reference>). Besides Ephesus, from its position in Asia, its notorious voluptuousness and sorcery (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.18">Ac 19:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.19">19</reference>), and its lewd worship of Diana (answering to the Phoenician Ashtoreth), was likely from the first to tinge Christianity in some of its converts with Oriental speculations and Asiatic licentiousness of practices. Thus the phenomenon of the phase of error presented in this Epistle, being intermediate between Judaism and later Gnosticism (see above), would be such as might occur at an early period in the Ephesian Church, as well as later, when we know it had open "apostles" of error (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Re 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">6</reference>), and Nicolaitans infamous in practice. As to the close connection between this First Epistle and the Second Epistle (which must have been written at the close of Paul's life), on which Alford relies for his theory of making the First Epistle also written at the close of Paul's life, the similarity of circumstances, the person addressed being one and the same, and either in Ephesus at the time, or at least connected with Ephesus as its church overseer, and having heretics to contend with of the same stamp as in the First Epistle, would account for the connection. There is not so great identity of tone as to compel us to adopt the theory that some years could not have elapsed between the two Epistles.<div eID="gen37044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37045" type="x-p"/> However, all these arguments against the later date may be answered. This First Epistle may refer not to the first organization of the Church under its bishops, or elders and deacons, but to the moral qualifications laid down at a later period for those officers when scandals rendered such directions needful. Indeed, the object for which he left Timothy at Ephesus he states (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>) to be, not to organize the Church for the first time, but to restrain the false teachers. The directions as to the choice of fit elders and deacons refer to the filling up of vacancies, not to their first appointment. The fact of there existing an institution for Church widows implies an established organization. As to Timothy's "youth," it may be spoken of comparatively young compared with Paul, now "the aged" (Phm 9), and with some of the Ephesian elders, senior to Timothy their overseer. As to <reference osisRef="Acts.20.25">Ac 20:25</reference>, we know not but that "all" of the elders of Ephesus called to Miletus "never saw Paul's face" afterwards, as he "knew" (doubtless by inspiration) would be the case, which obviates the need of Alford's lax view, that Paul was wrong in this his positive inspired anticipation (for such it was, not a mere boding surmise as to the future). Thus he probably visited Ephesus again (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.20">4:20</reference>, he would hardly have been at Miletum, so near Ephesus, without visiting Ephesus) after his first imprisonment in Rome, though all the Ephesian elders whom he had addressed formerly at Miletus did not again see him. The general similarity of subject and style, and of the state of the Church between the two Epistles, favors the view that they were near one another in date. Also, against the theory of the early date is the difficulty of defining, when, during Paul's two or three years' stay at Ephesus, we can insert an absence of Paul from Ephesus long enough for the requirements of the case, which imply a lengthened stay and superintendence of Timothy at Ephesus (see, however, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Ti 3:14</reference>, on the other side) after having been "left" by Paul there. Timothy did not stay there when Paul left Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>). In <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Ti 3:14</reference>, Paul says, "I write, hoping to come unto thee shortly," but on the earlier occasion of his passing from Ephesus to Macedon he had no such expectation, but had planned to spend the summer in Macedon, and the winter in Corinth, (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.6">1Co 16:6</reference>). The expression "Till I come" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.13">1Ti 4:13</reference>), implies that Timothy was not to leave his post till Paul should arrive; this and the former objection, however, do not hold good against Mosheim's theory. Moreover, Paul in his farewell address to the Ephesian elders prophetically anticipates the rise of false teachers hereafter of their own selves; therefore this First Epistle, which speaks of their actual presence at Ephesus, would naturally seem to be not prior, but subsequent, to the address, that is, will belong to the later date assigned. In the Epistle to the Ephesians no notice is taken of the Judaeo-Gnostic errors, which would have been noticed had they been really in existence; however, they are alluded to in the contemporaneous sister Epistle to Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1-Col.2.23">Col 2:1-23</reference>).<div eID="gen37045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37046" type="x-p"/> Whatever doubt must always remain as to the date of the First Epistle, there can be hardly any as to that of the Second Epistle. In <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Ti 4:13</reference>, Paul directs Timothy to bring the books and cloak which the apostle had left at Troas. Assuming that the visit to Troas referred to is the one mentioned in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.5-Acts.20.7">Ac 20:5-7</reference>, it will follow that the cloak and parchments lay for about seven years at Troas, that being the time that elapsed between the visit and Paul's first imprisonment at Rome: a very unlikely supposition, that he should have left either unused for so long. Again, when, during his first Roman imprisonment, he wrote to the Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>) and Philemon (Phm 24), Demas was with him; but when he was writing <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>, Demas had forsaken him from love of this world, and gone to Thessalonica. Again, when he wrote to the Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, and Philemon, he had good hopes of a speedy liberation; but here in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6-2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:6-8</reference>, he anticipates immediate death, having been at least once already tried (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>). Again, he is in this Epistle represented as in closer confinement than he was when writing those former Epistles in his first imprisonment (even in the Philippians, which represent him in greater uncertainty as to his life, he cherished the hope of soon being delivered, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.24">Php 2:24</reference>; 2Ti 1:16-18; 2:9; 4:6-8, 16). Again (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), he speaks of having left Trophimus sick at Miletum. This could not have been on the occasion, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.15">Ac 20:15</reference>. For Trophimus was with Paul at Jerusalem shortly afterwards (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.29">Ac 21:29</reference>). Besides, he would thus be made to speak of an event six or seven years after its occurrence, as a recent event: moreover, Timothy was, on that occasion of the apostle being at Miletum, with Paul, and therefore needed not to be informed of Trophimus' sickness there (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.4-Acts.20.17">Ac 20:4-17</reference>). Also, the statement (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), "Erastus abode at Corinth," implies that Paul had shortly before been at Corinth, and left Erastus there; but Paul had not been at Corinth for several years before his first imprisonment, and in the interval Timothy had been with him, so that he did not need to write subsequently about that visit. He must therefore have been liberated after his first imprisonment (indeed, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.23">He 13:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.24">24</reference>, expressly proves that the writer was in Italy and at liberty), and resumed his apostolic journeyings, and been imprisoned at Rome again, whence shortly before his death he wrote Second Timothy.<div eID="gen37046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37047" type="x-p"/> Eusebius [Chronicles, Anno 2083] (beginning October, A.D. 67), says, "Nero, to his other crimes, added the persecution of Christians: under him the apostles Peter and Paul consummated their martyrdom at Rome." So Jerome [On Illustrious Men], "In the fourteenth year of Nero, Paul was beheaded at Rome for Christ's sake, on the same day as Peter, and was buried on the Ostian Road, in the thirty-seventh year after the death of our Lord." Alford reasonably conjectures the Pastoral Epistles were written near this date. The interval was possibly filled up (so Clement of Rome states that Paul preached as far as "to the extremity of the west") by a journey to Spain (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.24">Ro 15:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.28">28</reference>), according to his own original intention. Muratori's Fragment on the Canon of Scripture (about A.D. 170) also alleges Paul's journey into Spain. So Eusebius, Chrysostom, and Jerome. Be that as it may, he seems shortly before his second imprisonment to have visited Ephesus, where a new body of elders governed the Church (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.25">Ac 20:25</reference>), say in the latter end of A.D. 66, or beginning of 67. Supposing him thirty at his conversion, he would now be upwards of sixty, and older in constitution than in years, through continual hardship. Even four years before he called himself "Paul the aged" (Phm 9).<div eID="gen37047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37048" type="x-p"/> From Ephesus he went into Macedonia (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>). He may have written the First Epistle to Timothy from that country. But his use of "went," not "came," in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>, "When I went into Macedonia," implies he was not there when writing. Wherever he was, he writes uncertain how long he may be detained from coming to Timothy (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Ti 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">15</reference>). Birks shows the probability that he wrote from Corinth, between which city and Ephesus the communication was rapid and easy. His course, as on both former occasions, was from Macedon to Corinth. He finds a coincidence between <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11-1Tim.2.14">1Ti 2:11-14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>, as to women being silent in Church; and <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.18">18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.8-1Cor.9.10">1Co 9:8-10</reference>, as to the maintenance of ministers, on the same principle as the Mosaic law, that the ox should not be muzzled that treadeth out the corn; and <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.20">20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.1-2Cor.13.4">2Co 13:1-4</reference>, as to charges against elders. It would be natural for the apostle in the very place where these directions had been enforced, to reproduce them in his letter.<div eID="gen37048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37049" type="x-p"/> The date of the Epistle to Titus must depend on that assigned to First Timothy, with which it is connected in subject, phraseology, and tone. There is no difficulty in the Epistle to Titus, viewed by itself, in assigning it to the earlier date, namely, before Paul's first imprisonment. In <reference osisRef="Acts.18.18">Ac 18:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19">19</reference>, Paul, in journeying from Corinth to Palestine, for some cause or other landed at Ephesus. Now we find (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.13">Tit 3:13</reference>) that Apollos in going from Ephesus to Corinth was to touch at Crete (which seems to coincide with Apollos' journey from Ephesus to Corinth, recorded in <reference osisRef="Acts.18.24">Ac 18:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.19.1">19:1</reference>); therefore it is not unlikely that Paul may have taken Crete similarly on his way between Corinth and Ephesus; or, perhaps been driven out of his course to it in one of his three shipwrecks spoken of in <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.25">2Co 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">26</reference>; this will account for his taking Ephesus on his way from Corinth to Palestine, though out of his regular course. At Ephesus Paul may have written the Epistle to Titus [Hug]; there he probably met Apollos and gave the Epistle to Titus to his charge, before his departure for Corinth by way of Crete, and before the apostle's departure for Jerusalem (Ac 18:19-21, 24). Moreover, on Paul's way back from Jerusalem and Antioch, he travelled some time in Upper Asia (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.1">Ac 19:1</reference>); and it was then, probably, that his intention to "winter at Nicopolis" was realized, there being a town of that name between Antioch and Tarsus, lying on Paul's route to Galatia (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>). Thus, First Timothy will, in this theory, be placed two and a half years later (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.1">Ac 20:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37050" type="x-p"/> Alford's argument for classing the Epistle to Titus with First Timothy, as written after Paul's first Roman imprisonment, stands or falls with his argument for assigning First Timothy to that date. Indeed, Hug's unobjectionable argument for the earlier date of the Epistle to Titus, favors the early date assigned to First Timothy, which is so much akin to it, if other arguments be not thought to counterbalance this. The Church of Crete had been just founded (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit 1:5</reference>), and yet the same heresies are censured in it as in Ephesus, which shows that no argument, such as Alford alleges against the earlier date of First Timothy, can be drawn from them (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.10">Tit 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.15">11, 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">11</reference>). But vice versa, if, as seems likely from the arguments adduced, the First Epistle to Timothy be assigned to the later date, the Epistle to Titus must, from similarity of style, belong to the same period. Alford traces Paul's last journey before his second imprisonment thus: To Crete (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit 1:5</reference>), Miletus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), Colosse (fulfilling his intention, Phm 22), Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.18">2Ti 1:18</reference>), from which neighborhood he wrote the Epistle to Titus; Troas, Macedonia, Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.20">2Ti 4:20</reference>), Nicopolis (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.12">Tit 3:12</reference>) in Epirus, where he had intended to winter; a place in which, as being a Roman colony, he would be free from tumultuary violence, and yet would be more open to a direct attack from foes in the metropolis, Rome. Being known in Rome as the leader of the Christians, he was probably [Alford] arrested as implicated in causing the fire in A.D. 64, attributed by Nero to the Christians, and was sent to Rome by the Duumvirs of Nicopolis. There he was imprisoned as a common malefactor (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">2Ti 2:9</reference>); his Asiatic friends deserted him, except Onesiphorus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.16">2Ti 1:16</reference>). Demas, Crescens, and Titus, left him. Tychicus he had sent to Ephesus. Luke alone remained with him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10-2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:10-12</reference>). Under the circumstances he writes the Second Epistle to Timothy, most likely while Timothy was at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.13">2Ti 4:13</reference>), begging him to come to him before winter (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>), and anticipating his own execution soon (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6">2Ti 4:6</reference>). Tychicus was perhaps the bearer of the Second Epistle (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.12">2Ti 4:12</reference>). His defense was not made before the emperor, for the latter was then in Greece (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2Ti 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">17</reference>). Tradition represents that he died by the sword, which accords with the fact that his Roman citizenship would exempt him from torture; probably late in A.D. 67 or A.D. 68, the last year of Nero.<div eID="gen37050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37051" type="x-p"/> Timothy is first mentioned, <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>, as dwelling in Lystra (not Derbe, compare <reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>). His mother was a Jewess named Eunice (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>); his father, "a Greek" (that is, a Gentile). As Timothy is mentioned as "a disciple" in <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>, he must have been converted before, and this by Paul (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>), probably at his former visit to Lystra (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.6">Ac 14:6</reference>); at the same time, probably, that his Scripture-loving mother, Eunice, and grandmother, Lois, were converted to Christ from Judaism (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.14">2Ti 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">15</reference>). Not only the good report given as to him by the brethren of Lystra, but also his origin, partly Jewish, partly Gentile, adapted him specially for being Paul's assistant in missionary work, laboring as the apostle did in each place, firstly among the Jews, and then among the Gentiles. In order to obviate Jewish prejudices, he first circumcised him. He seems to have accompanied Paul in his tour through Macedonia; but when the apostle went forward to Athens, Timothy and Silas remained in Berea. Having been sent back by Paul to visit the Thessalonian Church (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.2">1Th 3:2</reference>), he brought his report of it to the apostle at Corinth (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.6">1Th 3:6</reference>). Hence we find his name joined with Paul's in the addresses of both the Epistles to Thessalonians, which were written at Corinth. We again find him "ministering to" Paul during the lengthened stay at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference>). Thence he was sent before Paul into Macedonia and to Corinth (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">16:10</reference>). He was with Paul when he wrote the Second Epistle to Corinthians (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>); and the following winter in Corinth, when Paul sent from thence his Epistle to the Romans (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Ro 16:21</reference>). On Paul's return to Asia through Macedonia, he went forward and waited for the apostle at Troas (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.3-Acts.20.5">Ac 20:3-5</reference>). Next we find him with Paul during his imprisonment at Rome, when the apostle wrote the Epistles to Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.1.1">Col 1:1</reference>), Philemon (Phm 1), and Philippians (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>). He was imprisoned and set at liberty about the same time as the writer of the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.23">He 13:23</reference>). In the Pastoral Epistles, we find him mentioned as left by the apostle at Ephesus to superintend the Church there (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>). The last notice of him is in the request which Paul makes to him (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.21">2Ti 4:21</reference>) to "come before winter," that is about A.D. 67 [Alford]. Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 3.42], reports that he was first bishop of Ephesus; and [NICOPHORUS, Ecclesiastical History, 3.11], represents that he died by martyrdom. If then, St. John, as tradition represents, resided and died in that city, it must have been at a later period. Paul himself ordained or consecrated him with laying on of his own hands, and those of the presbytery, in accordance with prophetic intimations given respecting him by those possessing the prophetic gift (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">4:14</reference> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference>). His self-denying character is shown by his leaving home at once to accompany the apostle, and submitting to circumcision for the Gospel's sake; and also by his abstemiousness (noted in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Ti 5:23</reference>) notwithstanding his bodily infirmities, which would have warranted a more generous diet. Timidity and a want of self-confidence and boldness in dealing with the difficulties of his position, seem to have been a defect in his otherwise beautiful character as a Christian minister (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1Co 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>).<div eID="gen37051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37052" type="x-p"/> The DESIGN of the First Epistle was: (1) to direct Timothy to charge the false teachers against continuing to teach other doctrine than that of the Gospel (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3-1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:3-20</reference>; compare Re 2:1-6); (2) to give him instructions as to the orderly conducting of worship, the qualifications of bishops and deacons, and the selection of widows who should, in return for Church charity, do appointed service (1Ti 2:<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1-6:2</reference>); (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.3">3</reference>) to warn against covetousness, a sin prevalent at Ephesus, and to urge to good works (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3-1Tim.6.19">1Ti 6:3-19</reference>).<div eID="gen37052" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen37053" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1-1Tim.1.20">1Ti 1:1-20</reference>. Address: Paul's Design in Having Left Timothy at Ephesus, Namely, to Check False Teachers; True Use of the Law; Harmonizing with the Gospel; God's Grace in Calling Paul, Once a Blasphemer, to Experience and to Preach It; Charges to Timothy.<div eID="gen37053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18056"/><hi type="bold">1. by the commandment of God--</hi>the authoritative injunction, as well as the commission, of God. In the earlier Epistles the phrase is, "by the will of God." Here it is expressed in a manner implying that a necessity was laid on him to act as an apostle, not that it was merely at his option. The same expression occurs in the doxology, probably written long after the Epistle itself [Alford] (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.26">Ro 16:26</reference>).<div eID="gen37054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God our Saviour--</hi>The Father (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.3">1Ti 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.47">Lu 1:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference>; 2:10; 3:4; Jude 25). It was a Jewish expression in devotion, drawn from the Old Testament (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.106.21">Psa 106:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our hope--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>; 2:13). <div eID="gen37056" type="x-p"/>
entries.dea845eae96a5a2664d4d8745268929b61952638: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18057"/><div sID="gen37057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18057"/><hi type="bold">2. my own son--</hi>literally, "a genuine son" (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14-1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:14-17</reference>). See Introduction.<div eID="gen37057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercy--</hi>added here, in addressing Timothy, to the ordinary salutation, "Grace unto you (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Ro 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">1Co 1:3</reference>, &c.), and peace." In <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Ga 6:16</reference>, "peace and mercy" occur. There are many similarities of style between the Epistle to the Galatians and the Pastoral Epistles (see Introduction); perhaps owing to his there, as here, having, as a leading object in writing, the correction of false teachers, especially as to the right and wrong use of the law (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>). If the earlier date be assigned to First Timothy, it will fall not long after, or before (according as the Epistle to the Galatians was written at Ephesus or at Corinth) the writing of the Epistle to the Galatians, which also would account for some similarity of style. "Mercy" is grace of a more tender kind, exercised towards the miserable, the experience of which in one's own case especially fits for the Gospel MINISTRY. Compare as to Paul himself (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.14">1Ti 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.25">1Co 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">2Co 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.17">He 2:17</reference>) [Bengel]. He did not use "mercy" as to the churches, because "mercy" in all its fulness already existed towards them; but in the case of an individual minister, fresh measures of it were continually needed. "Grace" has reference to the sins of men; "mercy" to their misery. God extends His grace to men as they are guilty; His "mercy" to them as they are miserable [Trench].<div eID="gen37058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read the order, "Christ Jesus." In the Pastoral Epistles "Christ" is often put before "Jesus," to give prominence to the fact that the Messianic promises of the Old Testament, well known to Timothy (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Ti 3:15</reference>), were fulfilled in Jesus. <div eID="gen37059" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf1e08601505ee3a3959b39c548fb8ac5f764edc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18058"/><div sID="gen37060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18058"/>3. Timothy's superintendence of the Church at Ephesus was as locum tenens for the apostle, and so was temporary. Thus, the office of superintending overseer, needed for a time at Ephesus or Crete, in the absence of the presiding apostle, subsequently became a permanent institution on the removal, by death, of the apostles who heretofore superintended the churches. The first title of these overseers seems to have been "angels" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Re 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen37060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">As I besought thee to abide still--</hi>He meant to have added, "so I still beseech thee," but does not complete the sentence until he does so virtually, not formally, at <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>.<div eID="gen37061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at Ephesus--</hi>Paul, in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.25">Ac 20:25</reference>, declared to the Ephesian elders, "I know that ye all shall see my face no more." If, then, as the balance of arguments seems to favor (see Introduction), this Epistle was written subsequently to Paul's first imprisonment, the apparent discrepancy between his prophecy and the event may be reconciled by considering that the terms of the former were not that he should never visit Ephesus again (which this verse implies he did), but that they all should "see his face no more." I cannot think with Birks, that this verse is compatible with his theory, that Paul did not actually visit Ephesus, though in its immediate neighborhood (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Ti 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.13">4:13</reference>). The corresponding conjunction to "as" is not given, the sentence not being completed till it is virtually so at <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>.<div eID="gen37062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I besought--</hi>a mild word, instead of authoritative command, to Timothy, as a fellow helper.<div eID="gen37063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">some--</hi>The indefinite pronoun is slightly contemptuous as to them (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.12">Ga 2:12</reference>; Jude 4), [Ellicott].<div eID="gen37064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teach no other doctrine--</hi>than what I have taught (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.6-Gal.1.9">Ga 1:6-9</reference>). His prophetic bodings some years before (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.29">Ac 20:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">30</reference>) were now being realized (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>). <div eID="gen37065" type="x-p"/>
entries.690532ce83cb8910a10c0c006176b1487ffae6af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18059"/><div sID="gen37066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18059"/><hi type="bold">4. fables--</hi>legends about the origin and propagation of angels, such as the false teachers taught at Colosse (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18-Col.2.23">Col 2:18-23</reference>). "Jewish fables" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>). "Profane, and old wives' fables" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">1Ti 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.4">2Ti 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">genealogies--</hi>not merely such civil genealogies as were common among the Jews, whereby they traced their descent from the patriarchs, to which Paul would not object, and which he would not as here class with "fables," but Gnostic genealogies of spirits and aeons, as they called them, "Lists of Gnostic emanations" [Alford]. So Tertullian [Against Valentinian, c. 3], and Irenæus [Preface]. The Judaizers here alluded to, while maintaining the perpetual obligation of the Mosaic law, joined with it a theosophic ascetic tendency, pretending to see in it mysteries deeper than others could see. The seeds, not the full-grown Gnosticism of the post-apostolic age, then existed. This formed the transition stage between Judaism and Gnosticism. "Endless" refers to the tedious unprofitableness of their lengthy genealogies (compare <reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>). Paul opposes to their "aeons," the "King of the aeons (so the Greek, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">1Ti 1:17</reference>), whom be glory throughout the aeons of aeons." The word "aeons" was probably not used in the technical sense of the latter Gnostics as yet; but "the only wise God" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">1Ti 1:17</reference>), by anticipation, confutes the subsequently adopted notions in the Gnostics' own phraseology.<div eID="gen37067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">questions--</hi>of mere speculation (<reference osisRef="Acts.25.20">Ac 25:20</reference>), not practical; generating merely curious discussions.
