"Questions and strifes of words" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>): "to no profit" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Ti 2:14</reference>); "gendering strifes" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">2Ti 2:23</reference>). "Vain jangling" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.6">1Ti 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>) of would-be "teachers of the law."<div eID="gen37068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">godly edifying--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "the dispensation of God," the Gospel dispensation of God towards man (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.17">1Co 9:17</reference>), "which is (has its element) in faith." Conybeare translates, "The exercising of the stewardship of God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.17">1Co 9:17</reference>). He infers that the false teachers in Ephesus were presbyters, which accords with the prophecy, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">Ac 20:30</reference>. However, the oldest Latin versions, and Irenæus and Hilary, support English Version reading. Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>, "faith unfeigned." <div eID="gen37069" type="x-p"/>
entries.4db45234624a4afb8a1c675aa2c2d84337686c38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18060"/><div sID="gen37070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18060"/><hi type="bold">5. But--</hi>in contrast to the doctrine of the false teachers.<div eID="gen37070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the end--</hi>the aim.<div eID="gen37071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the commandment--</hi>Greek, "of the charge" which you ought to urge on your flock. Referring to the same Greek word as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>; here, however, in a larger sense, as including the Gospel "dispensation of God" (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.11">1Ti 1:11</reference>), which was the sum and substance of the "charge" committed to Timothy wherewith he should "charge" his flock.<div eID="gen37072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charity--</hi>LOVE; the sum and end of the law and of the Gospel alike, and that wherein the Gospel is the fulfilment of the spirit of the law in its every essential jot and tittle (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.10">Ro 13:10</reference>). The foundation is faith (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>), the "end" is love (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.14">1Ti 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.15">Tit 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of--</hi>springing as from a fountain.<div eID="gen37074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pure heart--</hi>a heart purified by faith (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.9">Ac 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Ti 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen37075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good conscience--</hi>a conscience cleared from guilt by the effect of sound faith in Christ (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">1Ti 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.9">1Ti 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.3">2Ti 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>). Contrast <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.2">1Ti 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.23.1">Ac 23:1</reference>. John uses "heart," where Paul would use "conscience." In Paul the understanding is the seat of conscience; the heart is the seat of love [Bengel]. A good conscience is joined with sound faith; a bad conscience with unsoundness in the faith (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">He 9:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith unfeigned--</hi>not a hypocritical, dead, and unfruitful faith, but faith working by love (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference>). The false teachers drew men off from such a loving, working, real faith, to profitless, speculative "questions" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>) and jangling (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.6">1Ti 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen37077" type="x-p"/>
entries.73e9c5ed6f32f712ab3dbbf0d1d55b2f2ae5f434: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18061"/><div sID="gen37078" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18061"/><hi type="bold">6. From which--</hi>namely, from a pure heart, good conscience, and faith unfeigned, the well-spring of love.<div eID="gen37078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having swerved--</hi>literally, "having missed the mark (the 'end') to be aimed at." It is translated, "erred," <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.21">1Ti 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>. Instead of aiming at and attaining the graces above named, they "have turned aside (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.15">1Ti 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.4">2Ti 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.13">He 12:13</reference>) unto vain jangling"; literally, "vain talk," about the law and genealogies of angels (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.9">Tit 3:9</reference>; 1:10); <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>, "vain babblings and oppositions." It is the greatest vanity when divine things are not truthfully discussed (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Ro 1:21</reference>) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37079" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffcf90ff0436ae97d6a8974a50882932f0b3d7ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18062"/><div sID="gen37080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18062"/>7. Sample of their "vain talk" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.6">1Ti 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen37080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Desiring--</hi>They are would-be teachers, not really so.<div eID="gen37081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the law--</hi>the Jewish law (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>). The Judaizers here meant seem to be distinct from those impugned in the Epistles to the Galatians and Romans, who made the works of the law necessary to justification in opposition to Gospel grace. The Judaizers here meant corrupted the law with "fables," which they pretended to found on it, subversive of morals as well as of truth. Their error was not in maintaining the obligation of the law, but in abusing it by fabulous and immoral interpretations of, and additions to, it.<div eID="gen37082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither what they say, nor whereof--</hi>neither understanding their own assertions, nor the object itself about which they make them. They understand as little about the one as the other [Alford]. <div eID="gen37083" type="x-p"/>
entries.394e08a8e4f5a55608c5d91ef5efc150bb679214: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18063"/><div sID="gen37084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18063"/><hi type="bold">8. But--</hi>"Now we know" (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.19">Ro 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">7:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law is good--</hi>in full agreement with God's holiness and goodness.<div eID="gen37085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if a man--</hi>primarily, a teacher; then, every Christian.<div eID="gen37086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">use it lawfully--</hi>in its lawful place in the Gospel economy, namely, not as a means of a "'righteous man" attaining higher perfection than could be attained by the Gospel alone (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>), which was the perverted use to which the false teachers put it, but as a means of awakening the sense of sin in the ungodly (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7-Rom.7.12">Ro 7:7-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">Ga 3:21</reference>). <div eID="gen37087" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a65353e09c971ba6c65e53b7bd999076be0fd43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18064"/><div sID="gen37088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18064"/><hi type="bold">9. law is not made for a righteous man--</hi>not for one standing by faith in the righteousness of Christ put on him for justification, and imparted inwardly by the Spirit for sanctification. "One not forensically amenable to the law" [Alford]. For sanctification, the law gives no inward power to fulfil it; but Alford goes too far in speaking of the righteous man as "not morally needing the law." Doubtless, in proportion as he is inwardly led by the Spirit, the justified man needs not the law, which is only an outward rule (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.14">Ro 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.18">Ga 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.23">23</reference>). But as the justified man often does not give himself up wholly to the inward leading of the Spirit, he morally needs the outward law to show him his sin and God's requirements. The reason why the ten commandments have no power to condemn the Christian, is not that they have no authority over him, but because Christ has fulfilled them as our surety (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">Ro 10:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">disobedient--</hi>Greek, "not subject"; insubordinate; it is translated "unruly," <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>; "lawless and disobedient" refer to opposers of the law, for whom it is "enacted" (so the Greek, for "is made").<div eID="gen37089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ungodly and ... sinners--</hi>Greek, he who does not reverence God, and he who openly sins against Him; the opposers of God, from the law comes.<div eID="gen37090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unholy and profane--</hi>those inwardly impure, and those deserving exclusion from the outward participation in services of the sanctuary; sinners against the third and fourth commandments.<div eID="gen37091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">murderers--</hi>or, as the Greek may mean, "smiters" of fathers and ... mothers; sinners against the fifth commandment.<div eID="gen37092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manslayers--</hi>sinners against the sixth commandment. <div eID="gen37093" type="x-p"/>
entries.28b9e2bd482a3a22c4e9eaf56ea604fa85edb072: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18065"/><div sID="gen37094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18065"/><hi type="bold">10. whoremongers, &c.--</hi>sinners against the seventh commandment.<div eID="gen37094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men-stealers--</hi>that is, slave dealers. The most heinous offense against the eighth commandment. No stealing of a man's goods can equal in atrocity the stealing of a man's liberty. Slavery is not directly assailed in the New Testament; to have done so would have been to revolutionize violently the existing order of things. But Christianity teaches principles sure to undermine, and at last overthrow it, wherever Christianity has had its natural development (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.12">Mt 7:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">liars ... perjured--</hi>offenders against the ninth commandment.<div eID="gen37096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if there be any other thing--</hi>answering to the tenth commandment in its widest aspect. He does not particularly specify it because his object is to bring out the grosser forms of transgression; whereas the tenth is deeply spiritual, so much so indeed, that it was by it that the sense of sin, in its subtlest form of "lust," Paul tells us (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.7">Ro 7:7</reference>), was brought home to his own conscience. Thus, Paul argues, these would-be teachers of the law, while boasting of a higher perfection through it, really bring themselves down from the Gospel elevation to the level of the grossly "lawless," for whom, not for Gospel believers, the law was designed. And in actual practice the greatest sticklers for the law as the means of moral perfection, as in this case, are those ultimately liable to fall utterly from the morality of the law. Gospel grace is the only true means of sanctification as well as of justification.<div eID="gen37097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sound--</hi>healthy, spiritually wholesome (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.13">2Ti 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.13">Tit 1:13</reference>; 2:2), as opposed to sickly, morbid (as the Greek of "doting" means, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>), and "canker" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>). "The doctrine," or "teaching, which is according to godliness" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>). <div eID="gen37098" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c3567f8af687c04f057cc27c9cd2b7d987cc21d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18066"/><div sID="gen37099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18066"/><hi type="bold">11. According to the glorious gospel--</hi>The Christian's freedom from the law as a sanctifier, as well as a justifier, implied in the previous, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>, is what this <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.11">1Ti 1:11</reference> is connected with. This exemption of the righteous from the law, and assignment of it to the lawless as its true object, is "according to the Gospel of the glory (so the Greek, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>) of the blessed God." The Gospel manifests God's glory (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">Ep 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">3:16</reference>) in accounting "righteous" the believer, through the righteousness of Christ, without "the law" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>); and in imparting that righteousness whereby he loathes all those sins against which (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>) the law is directed. The term, "blessed," indicates at once immortality and supreme happiness. The supremely blessed One is He from whom all blessedness flows. This term, as applied to God, occurs only here and in <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>: appropriate in speaking here of the Gospel blessedness, in contrast to the curse on those under the law (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Ga 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">committed to my trust--</hi>Translate as in the Greek order, which brings into prominent emphasis Paul, "committed in trust to me"; in contrast to the kind of law-teaching which they (who had no Gospel commission), the false teachers, assumed to themselves (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.8">1Ti 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.3">Tit 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen37100" type="x-p"/>
entries.b67639e2dafc08584b0032c8e2866e827ac9a8f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18067"/><div sID="gen37101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18067"/>12. The honor done him in having the Gospel ministry committed to him suggests the digression to what he once was, no better (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:13</reference>) than those lawless ones described above (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.9">1Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>), when the grace of our Lord (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.14">1Ti 1:14</reference>) visited him.<div eID="gen37101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And--</hi>omitted in most (not all) of the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen37102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I thank--</hi>Greek, "I have (that is, feel) gratitude."<div eID="gen37103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enabled me--</hi>the same Greek verb as in <reference osisRef="Acts.9.22">Ac 9:22</reference>, "Saul increased the more in strength." An undesigned coincidence between Paul and Luke, his companion. Enabled me, namely, for the ministry. "It is not in my own strength that I bring this doctrine to men, but as strengthened and nerved by Him who saved me" [Theodoret]. Man is by nature "without strength" (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.6">Ro 5:6</reference>). True conversion and calling confer power [Bengel].<div eID="gen37104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for that--</hi>the main ground of his "thanking Christ."<div eID="gen37105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he counted me faithful--</hi>He foreordered and foresaw that I would be faithful to the trust committed to me. Paul's thanking God for this shows that the merit of his faithfulness was due solely to God's grace, not to his own natural strength (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.25">1Co 7:25</reference>). Faithfulness is the quality required in a steward (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">1Co 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">putting me into--</hi>rather as in <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.9">1Th 5:9</reference>, "appointing me (in His sovereign purposes of grace) unto the ministry" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Ac 20:24</reference>). <div eID="gen37107" type="x-p"/>
entries.a36568ab3c9b47882c43e30abb273511e88bf6a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18068"/><div sID="gen37108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18068"/><hi type="bold">13. Who was before--</hi>Greek, "Formerly being a blasphemer." "Notwithstanding that I was before a blasphemer," &c. (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.9">Ac 26:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen37108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">persecutor--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gal.1.13">Ga 1:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">injurious--</hi>Greek, "insulter"; one who acts injuriously from arrogant contempt of others. Translate, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.30">Ro 1:30</reference>, "despiteful." One who added insult to injury. Bengel translates, "a despiser." I prefer the idea, contumelious to others [Wahl]. Still I agree with Bengel that "blasphemer" is against God, "persecutor," against holy men, and "insolently injurious" includes, with the idea of injuring others, that of insolent "uppishness" [Donaldson] in relation to one's self. This threefold relation to God, to one's neighbor, and to one's self, occurs often in this Epistle (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.14">9, 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.12">Tit 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I obtained mercy--</hi>God's mercy, and Paul's want of it, stand in sharp contrast [Ellicott]; Greek, "I was made the object of mercy." The sense of mercy was perpetual in the mind of the apostle (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Ti 1:2</reference>). Those who have felt mercy can best have mercy on those out of the way (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.2">He 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen37111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because I did it ignorantly--</hi>Ignorance does not in itself deserve pardon; but it is a less culpable cause of unbelief than pride and wilful hardening of one's self against the truth (<reference osisRef="John.9.41">Joh 9:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.9">Ac 26:9</reference>). Hence it is Christ's plea of intercession for His murderers (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Lu 23:34</reference>); and it is made by the apostles a mitigating circumstance in the Jews' sin, and one giving a hope of a door of repentance (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">Ac 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Ro 10:2</reference>). The "because," &c., does not imply that ignorance was a sufficient reason for mercy being bestowed; but shows how it was possible that such a sinner could obtain mercy. The positive ground of mercy being shown to him, lies solely in the compassion of God (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>). The ground of the ignorance lies in the unbelief, which implies that this ignorance is not unaccompanied with guilt. But there is a great difference between his honest zeal for the law, and a wilful striving against the Spirit of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.24-Matt.12.32">Mt 12:24-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.52">Lu 11:52</reference>) [Wiesinger]. <div eID="gen37112" type="x-p"/>
entries.330f73c60ac1ea7dc38b0fc5fe5a2a4b7510aef3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18069"/><div sID="gen37113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18069"/><hi type="bold">14. And--</hi>Greek, "But." Not only so (was mercy shown me), but<div eID="gen37113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the grace--</hi>by which "I obtained mercy" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was exceeding abundant--</hi>Greek, "superabounded." Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound" (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Ro 5:20</reference>).<div eID="gen37115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with faith--</hi>accompanied with faith, the opposite of "unbelief" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love--</hi>in contrast to "a blasphemer, persecutor, and injurious."<div eID="gen37117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is in Christ--</hi>as its element and home [Alford]: here as its source whence it flows to us. <div eID="gen37118" type="x-p"/>
entries.f629770fd69a118bc74d88a11e67e0f8d364aafd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18070"/><div sID="gen37119" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18070"/><hi type="bold">15. faithful--</hi>worthy of credit, because "God" who says it "is faithful" to His word (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.24">1Th 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.3">2Th 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.5">Re 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.6">22:6</reference>). This seems to have become an axiomatic saying among Christians the phrase, "faithful saying," is peculiar to the Pastoral Epistles (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">Tit 3:8</reference>). Translate as Greek, "Faithful is the saying."<div eID="gen37119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>all possible; full; to be received by all, and with all the faculties of the soul, mind, and heart. Paul, unlike the false teachers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.7">1Ti 1:7</reference>), understands what he is saying, and whereof he affirms; and by his simplicity of style and subject, setting forth the grand fundamental truth of salvation through Christ, confutes the false teachers' abstruse and unpractical speculations (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18-1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:18-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.1">Tit 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">acceptation--</hi>reception (as of a boon) into the heart, as well as the understanding, with all gladness; this is faith acting on the Gospel offer, and welcoming and appropriating it (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.41">Ac 2:41</reference>).<div eID="gen37121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Christ--</hi>as promised.<div eID="gen37122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus--</hi>as manifested [Bengel].<div eID="gen37123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came into the world--</hi>which was full of sin (<reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.2">1Jo 2:2</reference>). This implies His pre-existence. <reference osisRef="John.1.9">Joh 1:9</reference>, Greek, "the true Light that, coming into the world, lighteth every man."<div eID="gen37124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to save sinners--</hi>even notable sinners like Saul of Tarsus. His instance was without a rival since the ascension, in point of the greatness of the sin and the greatness of the mercy: that the consenter to Stephen, the proto-martyr's death, should be the successor of the same!<div eID="gen37125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am--</hi>not merely, "I was chief" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.9">1Co 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Ep 3:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Lu 18:13</reference>). To each believer his own sins must always appear, as long as he lives, greater than those of others, which he never can know as he can know his own.<div eID="gen37126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief--</hi>the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:16</reference>, "first," which alludes to this fifteenth verse, Translate in both verses, "foremost." Well might he infer where there was mercy for him, there is mercy for all who will come to Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.11">Mt 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.10">Lu 19:10</reference>). <div eID="gen37127" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ace31c46790977819ff52df775926c3faf31cd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18071"/><div sID="gen37128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18071"/><hi type="bold">16. Howbeit--</hi>Greek, "But"; contrasting his own conscious sinfulness with God's gracious visitation of him in mercy.<div eID="gen37128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for this cause--</hi>for this very purpose.<div eID="gen37129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that in me--</hi>in my case.<div eID="gen37130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first--</hi>"foremost." As I was "foremost" (Greek for chief, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>) in sin, so God has made me the "foremost" sample of mercy.<div eID="gen37131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">show--</hi>to His own glory (the middle Greek, voice), <reference osisRef="Eph.2.7">Ep 2:7</reference>.<div eID="gen37132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all long-suffering--</hi>Greek, "the whole (of His) long-suffering," namely, in bearing so long with me while I was a persecutor.<div eID="gen37133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a pattern--</hi>a sample (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.6">1Co 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.11">11</reference>) to assure the greatest sinners of the certainty that they shall not be rejected in coming to Christ, since even Saul found mercy. So David made his own case of pardon, notwithstanding the greatness of his sin, a sample to encourage other sinners to seek pardon (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">Psa 32:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">6</reference>). The Greek for "pattern" is sometimes used for a "sketch" or outline--the filling up to take place in each man's own case.<div eID="gen37134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believe on him--</hi>Belief rests ON Him as the only foundation on which faith relies.<div eID="gen37135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to life everlasting--</hi>the ultimate aim which faith always keeps in view (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.2">Tit 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen37136" type="x-p"/>
entries.c66e579f83ec94d2c12db83fa21e6b2d9c3e2264: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18072"/><div sID="gen37137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18072"/>17. A suitable conclusion to the beautifully simple enunciation of the Gospel, of which his own history is a living sample or pattern. It is from the experimental sense of grace that the doxology flows [Bengel].<div eID="gen37137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the King, eternal--</hi>literally, "King of the (eternal) ages." The Septuagint translates <reference osisRef="Exod.15.18">Ex 15:18</reference>, "The Lord shall reign for ages and beyond them." <reference osisRef="Ps.145.13">Psa 145:13</reference>, Margin, "Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom," literally, "a kingdom of all ages." The "life everlasting" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:16</reference>) suggested here "the King eternal," or everlasting. It answers also to "for ever and ever" at the close, literally, "to the ages of the ages" (the countless succession of ages made up of ages).<div eID="gen37138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">immortal--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "incorruptible." The Vulgate, however, and one very old manuscript read as English Version (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.23">Ro 1:23</reference>).<div eID="gen37139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">invisible--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Ex 33:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">He 11:27</reference>).<div eID="gen37140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the only wise God--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "wise," which probably crept in from <reference osisRef="Rom.16.27">Ro 16:27</reference>, where it is more appropriate to the context than here (compare Jude 25). "The only Potentate" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.10">Psa 86:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>).<div eID="gen37141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37142" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever, &c.--</hi>See note, above. The thought of eternity (terrible as it is to unbelievers) is delightful to those assured of grace (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.16">1Ti 1:16</reference>) [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37142" type="x-p"/>
entries.eddec6192995cb78e3de5978522bc067ea71bbf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18073"/><div sID="gen37143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18073"/>18. He resumes the subject begun at <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>. The conclusion (apodosis) to the foregoing, "as I besought thee ... charge" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>), is here given, if not formally, at least substantially.<div eID="gen37143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This charge--</hi>namely, "that thou in them (so the Greek) mightest war," that is, fulfil thy high calling, not only as a Christian, but as a minister officially, one function of which is, to "charge some that they teach no other doctrine" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I commit--</hi>as a sacred deposit (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.2">2Ti 2:2</reference>) to be laid before thy hearers.<div eID="gen37145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to--</hi>in pursuance of; in consonance with.<div eID="gen37146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prophecies which went before on thee--</hi>the intimations given by prophets respecting thee at thy ordination, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference> (as, probably, by Silas, a companion of Paul, and "a prophet," <reference osisRef="Acts.15.32">Ac 15:32</reference>). Such prophetical intimation, as well as the good report given of Timothy by the brethren (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.2">Ac 16:2</reference>), may have induced Paul to take him as his companion. Compare similar prophecies as to others: <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1-Acts.13.3">Ac 13:1-3</reference>, in connection with laying on of hands; <reference osisRef="Acts.11.28">Ac 11:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.10">21:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.21.11">11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.10">1Co 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Ep 4:11</reference>. In <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>, it is expressly said that "the Holy Ghost had made them (the Ephesian presbyters) overseers." Clement of Rome [Epistle to the Corinthians], states it was the custom of the apostles "to make trial by the Spirit," that is, by the "power of discerning," in order to determine who were to be overseers and deacons in the several churches planted. So Clement of Alexandria says as to the churches near Ephesus, that the overseers were marked out for ordination by a revelation of the Holy Ghost to St. John.<div eID="gen37147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by them--</hi>Greek, "in them"; arrayed as it were in them; armed with them.<div eID="gen37148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">warfare--</hi>not the mere "fight" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">1Ti 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.7">2Ti 4:7</reference>), but the whole campaign; the military service. Translate as Greek, not "a," but "the good warfare." <div eID="gen37149" type="x-p"/>
entries.9784d4c838a60a30aa1509f9fd7859034d1eae00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18074"/><div sID="gen37150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18074"/><hi type="bold">19. Holding--</hi>Keeping hold of "faith" and "good conscience" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>); not "putting the latter away" as "some." Faith is like a very precious liquor; a good conscience is the clean, pure glass that contains it [Bengel]. The loss of good conscience entails the shipwreck of faith. Consciousness of sin (unrepented of and forgiven) kills the germ of faith in man [Wiesinger].<div eID="gen37150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>Greek singular, namely, "good conscience," not "faith" also; however, the result of putting away good conscience is, one loses faith also.<div eID="gen37151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put away--</hi>a wilful act. They thrust it from them as a troublesome monitor. It reluctantly withdraws, extruded by force, when its owner is tired of its importunity, and is resolved to retain his sin at the cost of losing it. One cannot be on friendly terms with it and with sin at one and the same time.<div eID="gen37152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made shipwreck--</hi>"with respect to THE faith." Faith is the vessel in which they had professedly embarked, of which "good conscience" is the anchor. The ancient Church often used this image, comparing the course of faith to navigation. The Greek does not imply that one having once had faith makes shipwreck of it, but that they who put away good conscience "make shipwreck with respect to THE faith." <div eID="gen37153" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a6d1690045519f583ebd1ad487b4346556f3d7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18075"/><div sID="gen37154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18075"/><hi type="bold">20. Hymenaeus--</hi>There is no difficulty in supposing him to be the Hymenæus of <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>. Though "delivered over to Satan" (the lord of all outside the Church, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Ac 26:18</reference>, and the executor of wrath, when judicially allowed by God, on the disobedient, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">1Co 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>), he probably was restored to the Church subsequently, and again troubled it. Paul, as an apostle, though distant at Rome pronounced the sentence to be executed at Ephesus, involving, probably, the excommunication of the offenders (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.17">Mt 18:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.18">18</reference>). The sentence operated not only spiritually, but also physically, sickness, or some such visitation of God, falling on the person excommunicated, in order to bring him to repentance and salvation. Alexander here is probably "the coppersmith" who did Paul "much evil" when the latter visited Ephesus. The "delivering him to Satan" was probably the consequence of his withstanding the apostle (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14">2Ti 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.15">15</reference>); as the same sentence on Hymenæus was the consequence of "saying that the resurrection is past already" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>; his putting away good conscience, naturally producing shipwreck concerning FAITH, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.19">1Ti 1:19</reference>. If one's religion better not his morals, his moral deficiencies will corrupt his religion. The rain which falls pure from heaven will not continue pure if it be received in an unclean vessel [Archbishop Whately]). It is possible that he is the Alexander, then a Jew, put forward by the Jews, doubtless against Paul, at the riot in Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.33">Ac 19:33</reference>).<div eID="gen37154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may--</hi>not "might"; implying that the effect still continues--the sentence is as yet unremoved.<div eID="gen37155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">learn--</hi>Greek, "be disciplined," namely, by chastisement and suffering.<div eID="gen37156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blaspheme--</hi>the name of God and Christ, by doings and teachings unworthy of their Christian profession (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.23">Ro 2:23</reference>, 24; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.7">Jas 2:7</reference>). Though the apostles had the power of excommunication, accompanied with bodily inflictions, miraculously sent (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.8">2Co 10:8</reference>), it does not follow that fallible ministers now have any power, save that of excluding from church fellowship notorious bad livers. <chapter eID="1Tim.1"/>

entries.9446dd003ca1734dfb94c68983155bf471144225: <div eID="gen51437" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to Timothy</title> <div sID="gen51438" type="x-p"/> In order to find out who this person was, it will be necessary to consult the Acts of the Apostles, where the first mention is made of him; and by collating what is there said with certain passages in the epistle, we shall find who he was, and the probable time in which the epistle was addressed to him. <div eID="gen51438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51439" type="x-p"/> Paul and Barnabas, in the course of their first apostolic journey among the Gentiles, came to Lystra, a city of Lycaonia, where they preached the Gospel for some time, and, though persecuted, with considerable success. See <reference osisRef="Act.14.5">Act 14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.14.6">Act 14:6</reference>. It is very likely that here they converted to the Christian faith a Jewess named Lois, with her daughter Eunice, who had married a Gentile, by whom she had Timothy, and whose father was probably at this time dead; the grandmother, daughter, and son living together. <div eID="gen51439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51440" type="x-p"/> Compare <reference osisRef="Act.16.1-Act.16.3">Act 16:1-3</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Tim 1:5</reference>. It is likely that Timothy was the only child; and it appears that he had been brought up in the fear of God, and carefully instructed in the Jewish religion by means of the Holy Scriptures. Compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Tim 1:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.15">2Tim 3:15</reference>. It appears, also, that this young man drank into the apostle's spirit, became a thorough convert to the Christian faith, and that a very tender intimacy subsisted between St. Paul and him. <div eID="gen51440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51441" type="x-p"/> When the apostle came from Antioch, in Syria, the second time to Lystra, he found Timothy a member of the Church, and so highly reputed and warmly recommended by the Church in that place, that St. Paul took him to be his companion in his travels. <reference osisRef="Act.16.1-Act.16.3">Act 16:1-3</reference>. From this place we learn that, although Timothy had been educated in the Jewish faith, he had not been circumcised, because his father, who was a Gentile, would not permit it. When the apostle had determined to take him with him, he found it necessary to have him circumcised, not from any supposition that circumcision was necessary to salvation, but because of the Jews, who would neither have heard him nor the apostle had not this been done: the Gospel testimony they would not have received from Timothy, because a heathen; and they would have considered the apostle in the same light, because he associated with such. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Act.16.3">Act 16:3</reference>. <div eID="gen51441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51442" type="x-p"/> It is pretty evident that Timothy had a special call of God to the work of an evangelist, which the elders of the Church at Lystra knowing, set him solemnly apart to the work by the imposition of hands; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Tim 4:14</reference>. And they were particularly led to this by several prophetic declarations relative to him, by which his Divine call was most clearly ascertained. See <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Tim 1:18</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Tim 3:14</reference>. Some think that, after this appointment by the elders, the apostle himself laid his hands on him, not for the purpose of his evangelical designation, but that he might receive those extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit so necessary in those primitive times to demonstrate the truth of the Gospel. See <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Tim 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Tim 1:7</reference>. Yet, it is likely that Timothy had not two ordinations; one by the elders of Lystra, and another by the apostle; as it is most probable that St. Paul acted with that πρεσβυτεριον or eldership mentioned <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Tim 4:14</reference>, among whom, in the imposition of hands, he would undoubtedly act as chief. <div eID="gen51442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51443" type="x-p"/> Timothy, thus prepared to be the apostle's fellow laborer in the Gospel, accompanied him and Silas when they visited the Churches of Phrygia, and delivered to them the decrees of the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, freeing the Gentiles from the law of Moses, as a term of salvation. Having gone through these countries, they at length came to Troas, where Luke joined them; as appears from the phraseology of his history, <reference osisRef="Act.16.10">Act 16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.16.11">Act 16:11</reference>, etc. In Troas a vision appeared to Paul, directing them to go into Macedonia. Loosing therefore from Troas, they all passed over to Neapolis; and from thence went to Philippi, where they converted many, and planted a Christian Church. From Philippi they went to Thessalonica, leaving Luke at Philippi; as appears from his changing the phraseology of his history at <reference osisRef="Act.16.40">Act 16:40</reference>. We may therefore suppose, that at their departing they committed the converted at Philippi to Luke's care. In Thessalonica they were opposed by the unbelieving Jews, and obliged to flee to Berea, whither the Jews from Thessalonica followed them. To elude their rage, Paul, who was most obnoxious to them, departed from Berea by night to go to Athens, leaving Silas and Timothy at Berea. At Athens, Timothy came to the apostle and gave him such an account of the afflicted state of the Thessalonian brethren, as induced him to send Timothy back to comfort them. After that Paul preached at Athens, hut with so little success that he judged it proper to leave Athens and go forward to Corinth, where Silas and Timothy came to him, and assisted in converting the Corinthians. And when he left Corinth they accompanied him, first to Ephesus, then to Jerusalem, and after that to Antioch, in Syria. Having spent some time in Antioch, Paul set out with Timothy on his third apostolical journey; in which, after visiting all the Churches of Galatia and Phrygia, in the order in which they had been planted, they came to Ephesus the second time, and there abode for a considerable time. In short, from the time Timothy first joined the apostle, as his assistant, he never left him except when sent by him on some special errand. And by his affection, fidelity, and zeal, he so recommended himself to all the disciples, and acquired such authority over them, that Paul inserted his name in the inscription of several of the letters which he wrote to the Churches, to show that their doctrine was one and the same. His esteem and affection for Timothy the apostle expressed still more conspicuously, by writing to him those excellent letters in the canon which bear his name; and which have been of the greatest use to the ministers of the Gospel ever since their publication, by directing them to discharge all the duties of their function in a proper manner. <div eID="gen51443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51444" type="x-p"/> The date of this epistle has been a subject of much controversy, some assigning it to the year 56, which is the common opinion; and others to 64 or 65. A great balance of probability appears to be in favor of this later date; and it appears to me that the arguments of Drs. Macknight and Paley are decisive in favor of the later date. The former, in his preface, gives a very clear view of the question. <div eID="gen51444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51445" type="x-p"/> In the third verse of the first chapter of this epistle the apostle says: "As I entreated thee to abide in Ephesus, when going into Macedonia, so do; that thou mayest charge some not to teach differently." From this it is plain, <div eID="gen51445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51446" type="x-p"/> 1. That Timothy was in Ephesus when the apostle wrote his first letter to him; <div eID="gen51446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51447" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had been left there by the apostle, who at parting with him entreated him to abide at Ephesus; <div eID="gen51447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51448" type="x-p"/> 3. That this happened when Paul was going from Ephesus to Macedonia; and, <div eID="gen51448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51449" type="x-p"/> 4. That he had entreated Timothy to abide in Ephesus, for the purpose of charging some teachers in that Church not to teach differently from the apostles. <div eID="gen51449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51450" type="x-p"/> In the history of the Acts of the Apostles there is no mention of Paul's going from Ephesus to Macedonia but once; viz. after the riot of Demetrius, <reference osisRef="Act.20.1">Act 20:1</reference>, for which reason Theodoret, among the ancients, and among the moderns, Estius, Baronius, Capellus, Grotius, Lightfoot, Salmasius, Hammond, Witsius, Lardner, Pearson, and others, have given it as their opinion, that the apostle speaks of that journey in his First Epistle to Timothy. Yet, if I am not mistaken, the following circumstance will show their opinion to be ill founded: - <div eID="gen51450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51451" type="x-p"/> 1. When the apostle went from Ephesus to Macedonia, as related <reference osisRef="Act.20.1">Act 20:1</reference>, Timothy was not in Ephesus, having gone from that city into Macedonia with Erastus by the apostle's direction; <reference osisRef="Act.19.22">Act 19:22</reference>. And in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, which was written after Timothy's departure from Ephesus, we are informed that he was to go from Macedonia to Corinth. <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Cor 4:17</reference> : "I have sent to you Timothy." <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.10">1Cor 16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.11">1Cor 16:11</reference> : "If Timothy be come, take care that he be among you without fear. Send him forward in peace, that he may come to me, for I expect him with the brethren." But before Timothy returned from Corinth, the apostle left Ephesus and went into Macedonia, where the brethren above mentioned met him, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Cor 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">2Cor 2:13</reference>, having Timothy in their company; as is plain from his joining the apostle in his Second Epistle to the Corinthians, which all agree was written from Macedonia, immediately after the brethren from Corinth gave the apostle an account of the success of his first letter. Wherefore, since Timothy was not in Ephesus when the apostle left the city after the riot, it could not be the occasion on which the apostle said to him: "As I entreated thee to abide in Ephesus, when going into Macedonia, so do." But the journey into Macedonia, of which he speaks, must have been some other journey not mentioned in the Acts. To remove this difficulty we are told that Timothy returned from Corinth to the apostle be lore his departure from Ephesus, and that he was left there after the riot; but that something happened, which occasioned him to follow the apostle into Macedonia; that there he joined him in writing his Second Epistle to the Corinthians; and, having finished his business in Macedonia, he returned to Ephesus and abode there, agreeably to the apostle's request. But as these suppositions are not warranted by the history of the Acts, Timothy's joining the apostle in his Second Epistle to the Corinthians may still be urged as a proof that he came with the brethren directly from Corinth to Macedonia. Farther, that Timothy did not go from Macedonia to Ephesus after joining the apostle in his Second Epistle to the Corinthians, but returned with him to Corinth to receive the collections, is, I think, plain from <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>, where he is mentioned as one of those who accompanied Paul from Corinth to Jerusalem with the collections. <div eID="gen51451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51452" type="x-p"/> 2. When the apostle wrote his First Epistle to Timothy, "he hoped to come to him soon," <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Tim 3:14</reference>; but from the history of the Acts it is certain that in no letter written to Timothy after the riot, till his first confinement in Rome, could the apostle say that he hoped to come to him soon. He could not say so in any letter written from Troas, the first place he stopped at after leaving Ephesus; for at that time he was going into Macedonia and Achaia to receive the collections for the poor from the Churches in these provinces. Neither could he say so after writing his Second Epistle to the Corinthians from Macedonia; for in that epistle he told the Corinthians he was coming to them with the Macedonian brethren, who were commissioned to attend him in his voyage to Jerusalem, with the collections, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.4">2Cor 9:4</reference>, and that he meant to sail directly from Corinth to Judea, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.16">2Cor 1:16</reference>. As little could he write to Timothy that he hoped to come to him soon, when he altered his resolution on the occasion of the lying in wait of the Jews, and returned into Macedonia, <reference osisRef="Act.20.3">Act 20:3</reference>. For he was then in such haste to be in Jerusalem on the day of pentecost, that when he came to Miletus, instead of going to Ephesus, he sent for the elders of that Church to come to him, <reference osisRef="Act.20.16">Act 20:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.20.17">Act 20:17</reference>. When he arrived in Judea, he could not write that he hoped to come to Ephesus soon, for he was imprisoned a few days after he went up to Jerusalem; and having continued two years in prison at Caesarea, he was sent bound to Rome, where likewise being confined, he could not, till towards the conclusion of that confinement, write to Timothy that he hoped to come to him soon. And even then he did not write his First Epistle to Timothy, for Timothy was with him at the conclusion of his confinement, <reference osisRef="Phi.2.19">Phi 2:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.2.23">Phi 2:23</reference>. <div eID="gen51452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51453" type="x-p"/> 3. From the first epistle we learn that the following were the errors Timothy was left in Ephesus to oppose: <div eID="gen51453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51454" type="x-p"/> 1. Fables invented by the Jewish doctors to recommend the observance of the law of Moses as necessary to salvation. <div eID="gen51454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51455" type="x-p"/> 2. Uncertain genealogies, by which individuals endeavored to trace their descent from Abraham, in the persuasion that they would be saved, merely because they had Abraham for their father. <div eID="gen51455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51456" type="x-p"/> 3. Intricate questions and strifes about some words in the law; perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, who reckoned that which produced most gain to be the best kind of godliness. <div eID="gen51456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51457" type="x-p"/> 4. Oppositions of knowledge, falsely so named. But these errors had not taken place in the Ephesian Church before the apostle's departure; for in his charge to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, he foretold that the false teachers were to enter in among them after his departing. <reference osisRef="Act.20.29">Act 20:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.20.30">Act 20:30</reference> : "I know that after my departing, shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things to draw away disciples after them." The same thing appears from the two epistles which the apostle wrote to the Corinthians; the one from Ephesus before the riot of Demetrius, the other from Macedonia after that event; and from the epistle which he wrote to the Ephesians themselves from Rome, during his confinement there. For in none of these letters is there any notice taken of the above mentioned errors, as subsisting among the Ephesians at the time they were written; which cannot be accounted for on supposition that they were prevalent in Ephesus when the apostle went into Macedonia after the riot. I am therefore of opinion that the first to Timothy, in which the apostle desired him to abide in Ephesus for the purpose of opposing the Judaizers and their errors, could not be written either from Troas or from Macedonia after the riot, as those who contend for the early date of the epistle suppose; but it must have been written some time after the apostle's release from confinement in Rome, when no doubt he visited the Church at Ephesus, and found the Judaizing teachers there busily employed in spreading their pernicious errors. <div eID="gen51457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51458" type="x-p"/> 4. In the first Epistle to Timothy the same sort of persons, doctrines, and practices, are reprobated, which are condemned in the second. Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.6">1Tim 4:1-6</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.5">2Tim 3:1-5</reference>; and <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Tim 6:20</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.14">2Tim 2:14</reference>; and <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Tim 6:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Tim 2:16</reference>. The same commands, instructions, and encouragements are given to Timothy in the first epistle as in the second. Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.13">1Tim 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14">1Tim 6:14</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.1-2Tim.4.5">2Tim 4:1-5</reference>. The same remedies for the corruptions which had taken place among the Ephesians are prescribed in the first epistle as in the second. Compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Tim 4:14</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Tim 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Tim 1:7</reference>; and as in the second epistle, so in the first, every thing is addressed to Timothy as superintendent both of the teachers and of the laity in the Church at Ephesus; all which, I think, imply that the state of things among the Ephesians was the same when the two epistles were written; consequently that the first epistle was written only a few months before the second, and not long before the apostle's death. <div eID="gen51458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51459" type="x-p"/> These arguments appeared so convincing to Pearson, Le Clerc, L'Enfant, Cave, Fabricius, Mill, Whitby, and others, that they were unanimously of opinion Timothy was left by the apostle in Ephesus as he went into Macedonia, not after the riot of Demetrius, but after he was released from his first confinement at Rome. And from that circumstance they infer that he did not write his first epistle till some time in the end of the year 64, or in the beginning of 65. I think it was written from Nicopolis. <div eID="gen51459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51460" type="x-p"/> To the late date of this first epistle, there are three plausible objections which must not be overlooked: - <div eID="gen51460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51461" type="x-p"/> 1. It is thought that, if the First Epistle to Timothy was written after the apostle's release, he could not with any propriety have said to Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Tim 4:12</reference> : "Let no man despise thy youth;" but it is replied: That Servius Tullius, in classing the Roman people, as Aulus Gellius relates, lib. x. c. 28, divided their age into three periods: Childhood he limited to the age of seventeen; youth, from that to forty-six; and old age, from that to the end of life. Now, supposing Timothy to have been eighteen years old, a.d. 50, when he became Paul's assistant, he would be no more than 32, a.d. 64, two years after the apostle's release, when it is supposed this epistle was written. Wherefore, being then in the period of life which, by the Greeks as well as the Roman, was considered as youth, the apostle with propriety might say to him, Let no man despise thy youth. <div eID="gen51461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51462" type="x-p"/> 2. When the apostle touched at Miletus, in his voyage to Jerusalem with the collections, the Church at Ephesus had a number of elders, that is, of bishops and deacons, who came to him at Miletus, <reference osisRef="Act.20.17">Act 20:17</reference>. It is therefore asked: What occasion was there in an epistle written after the apostle's release, to give Timothy directions concerning the ordination of bishops and deacons, in a Church where there were so many elders already? The answer is: The elders who came to the apostle at Miletus in the year 58 may have been too few for the Church at Ephesus, in her increased state, in the year 65. Besides, false teachers had then entered, to oppose whom more bishops and deacons might be needed than were necessary in the year 58; not to mention that some of the first elders having died, others were wanted to supply their places. <div eID="gen51462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51463" type="x-p"/> 3. Because the apostle wrote to Timothy that "he hoped to come to him soon," <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Tim 3:14</reference>, it is argued that the letter in which this is said must have been written before the apostle said to the Ephesian elders, <reference osisRef="Act.20.25">Act 20:25</reference> : "I know that ye all, among whom I have gone preaching the kingdom of God, shall see my face no more." But if, by this, the First Epistle to Timothy is proved to have been written before the apostle's interview with the elders at Miletus, his Epistles to the Philippians, to the Hebrews, and to Philemon, in which he promised to visit them, must likewise have been written before the interview; in regard, his declaration respected the Philippians, the Hebrews, and Philemon, as well as the Ephesians; for they certainly were persons among whom the apostle had gone preaching the kingdom of God. Yet no commentator ever thought the epistles above mentioned were written to them before the apostle's interview with the Ephesian elders; on the contrary, it is universally acknowledged that these epistles were written four years after the interview; namely, during the apostle's first imprisonment at Rome. Wherefore, when he told the Ephesian elders that they, and his other converts, among whom he had gone preaching the kingdom of God, should see his face no more, as it was no point either of faith or practice which he spake, he may well be supposed to have declared nothing but his own opinion, resulting from his fears. He had lately escaped the rage of the Jews, who laid wait for him in Cenchrea to kill him, <reference osisRef="Act.20.3">Act 20:3</reference>. This, with their fury on former occasions, filled him with such anxiety that, in writing to the Romans from Corinth; he requested them "to strive together with him in their prayers that he might be delivered from the unbelieving in Judea;" <reference osisRef="Rom.15.30">Rom 15:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.31">Rom 15:31</reference>. Farther, that in his own speech to the Ephesian elders the apostle only declared his own persuasion, dictated by his fears, and not any suggestion of the Spirit, I think plain from what he had said immediately before, <reference osisRef="Act.20.22">Act 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.20.23">Act 20:23</reference> : "Behold, I go bound in the spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing the things that shall befall me there: save that the Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions abide me." Wherefore, although his fears were happily disappointed, and he actually visited the Ephesians after his release; his character as an inspired apostle is not hurt in the least, if, in saying he knew they should see his face no more, he declared, as I have said, his own persuasion only, and no dictate of the Holy Ghost. <div eID="gen51463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51464" type="x-p"/> Dr. Paley's arguments are the same in substance; but he does not mention Dr. Macknight, who wrote before him, and whose work he must have seen. <div eID="gen51464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51465" type="x-p"/> The principal difficulty in this opinion is, that it necessarily implies that St. Paul visited Ephesus after his liberation at Rome; which appears so contrary to what he said to the Ephesian Church, that they should see his face no more. Dr. Paley, however, finds some farther presumptive evidences that the apostle must have visited Ephesus. The Epistles to the Philippians and to Philemon were written while the apostle was a prisoner at Rome; to the former he says: "I trust in the Lord, that I also myself shall come shortly;" and to the latter, who was a Colossian, he gives this direction: "But withal, prepare me also a lodging, for I trust that through your prayers I shall be given unto you." An inspection of the map will show us that Colosse was a city of Asia Minor, lying eastward, and at no great distance from Ephesus; Philippi was on the other, i.e. the western, side of the Aegean Sea. Now if the apostle executed his purpose, and came to Philemon at Colosse soon after his liberation, it cannot be supposed that he would omit to visit Ephesus, which lay so near it, and where he had spent three years of his ministry. As he was also under a promise to visit the Church at Philippi shortly, if he passed from Colosse to Philippi he could hardly avoid taking Ephesus in his way. See Paley's Horae Paulinae, page 293. This, taken in connection with the preceding arguments, can leave little doubt that the date of this epistle must be referred to a time subsequent to St. Paul's liberation from Rome, and consequently to the end of the year 64, or the beginning of the year 65. <div eID="gen51465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51466" type="x-p"/> Paul's salutation to Timothy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1Tim 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.2">1Tim 1:2</reference>. For what purpose he had left him at Ephesus, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Tim 1:3</reference>. What the false apostles taught in opposition to the truth, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4-1Tim.1.7">1Tim 1:4-7</reference>. The true use of the law, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.8-1Tim.1.11">1Tim 1:8-11</reference>. He thanks God for his own conversion, and describes his former state, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12-1Tim.1.17">1Tim 1:12-17</reference>. Exhorts Timothy to hold fast faith and a good conscience, and speaks of Hymeneus and Alexander who had made shipwreck of their faith, <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18-1Tim.1.20">1Tim 1:18-20</reference>. <div eID="gen51466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51467" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51468" type="x-p"/> Paul an apostle - by the commandment of God - We have already seen that the term αποστολος, apostle, literally signifies a person sent from one to another, without implying any particular dignity in the person, or importance in the message. But it is differently used in the New Testament, being applied to those who were sent expressly from God Almighty, with the message of salvation to mankind. It is, therefore, the highest character any human being can have; and he message is the most important which even God himself can send to his intelligent creatures. It was by the express command of God that St. Paul went to the Gentiles preaching the doctrine of salvation by faith in Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen51468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51469" type="x-p"/> Jesus Christ - our hope - Without Jesus, the world was hopeless; the expectation of being saved can only come to mankind by his Gospel. He is called our hope, as he is called our life, our peace, our righteousness, etc., because from him hope, life, peace, righteousness, and all other blessings proceed.
entries.e4da738c94bba0d4e0498f7141a63213c8bb2e78: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51470" type="x-p"/> My own son in the faith - Brought to salvation through Christ by my ministry alone. Probably the apostle speaks here according to this Jewish maxim: כל המלמר בן תכירו תורה מעלה עליו הכתוב כאלו ילרו He who teaches the law to his neighbour's son is considered by the Scripture as if he had begotten him; Sanhedrin, fol. xix. 2. And they quote <reference osisRef="Num.3.1">Num 3:1</reference>, as proving it: These are the generations of Aaron and Moses - and these are the names of the sons of Aaron. "Aaron," say they, "begot them, but Moses instructed them; therefore they are called by his name." See Schoettgen. <div eID="gen51470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51471" type="x-p"/> But γνησιῳ τεκνῳ may mean my beloved son; for in this sense το γνησιον is not unfrequently used. <div eID="gen51471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51472" type="x-p"/> In the faith - The word πιστις, faith, is taken here for the whole of the Christian religion, faith in Christ being its essential characteristic. <div eID="gen51472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51473" type="x-p"/> Grace, mercy, and peace - <div eID="gen51473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51474" type="x-p"/> Grace, the favor and approbation of God. <div eID="gen51474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51475" type="x-p"/> Mercy, springing from that grace, pardoning, purifying, and supporting. <div eID="gen51475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51476" type="x-p"/> Peace, the consequence of this manifested mercy, peace of conscience, and peace with God; producing internal happiness, quietness, and assurance.
entries.3b6160e987836dfc819efe159c4d23bd06e4d7b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51477" type="x-p"/> I besought thee - The apostle had seen that a bad seed had been sown in the Church; and, as he was obliged to go then into Macedonia, he wished Timothy, on whose prudence, piety, and soundness in the faith he could depend, to stay behind and prevent the spreading of a doctrine that would have been pernicious to the people's souls. I have already supposed that this epistle was written after Paul had been delivered from his first imprisonment at Rome, about the end of the year 64, or the beginning of 65. See the preface. When, therefore, the apostle came from Rome into Asia, he no doubt visited Ephesus, where, ten years before, he had planted a Christian Church, and, as he had not time to tarry then, he left Timothy to correct abuses. <div eID="gen51477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51478" type="x-p"/> That thou mightest charge some - He does not name any persons; the Judaizing teachers are generally supposed to be those intended; and the term τισι, some, certain persons, which he uses, is expressive of high disapprobation, and at the same time of delicacy: they were not apostles, nor apostolic men; but they were undoubtedly members of the Church at Ephesus, and might yet be reclaimed.
entries.ed62d4e4074613a7716874781bf005b4b198b059: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51479" type="x-p"/> Neither give heed to fables - Idle fancies; things of no moment; doctrines and opinions unauthenticated; silly legends, of which no people ever possessed a greater stock than the Jews. Their Talmud abounds with them; and the English reader may find them in abundance in Stehlin's Jewish Traditions, 2 vols. 8vo. <div eID="gen51479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51480" type="x-p"/> Endless genealogies - I suppose the apostle to mean those genealogies which were uncertain - that never could be made out, either in the ascending or descending line; and, principally, such as referred to the great promise of the Messiah, and to the priesthood. The Jews had scrupulously preserved their genealogical tables till the advent of Christ and the evangelists had recourse to them, and appealed to them in reference to our Lord's descent from the house of David; Matthew taking this genealogy in the descending, Luke in the ascending, line. And whatever difficulties we may now find in these genealogies, they were certainly clear to the Jews; nor did the most determined enemies of the Gospel attempt to raise one objection to it from the appeal which the evangelists had made to their own public and accredited tables. All was then certain; but we are told that Herod destroyed the public registers; he, being an Idumean, was jealous of the noble origin of the Jews; and, that none might be able to reproach him with his descent, be ordered the genealogical tables, which were kept among the archives in the temple, to be burnt. See Euseb. H. E., lib. i. cap. 8. From this time the Jews could refer to their genealogies only from memory, or from those imperfect tables which had been preserved in private hands; and to make out any regular line from these must have been endless and uncertain. It is probably to this that the apostle refers; I mean the endless and useless labor which the attempts to make out these genealogies must produce, the authentic tables being destroyed. This, were all other proofs wanting, would be an irresistible argument against the Jews that the Messiah is come; for their own prophets had distinctly marked out the line by which he was to come; the genealogies are now all lost; nor is there a Jew in the universe that can show from what tribe he is descended. There can, therefore, be no Messiah to come, as none could show, let him have what other pretensions he might, that he sprang from the house of David. The Jews do not, at present, pretend to have any such tables; and, far from being able to prove the Messiah from his descent, they are now obliged to say that, when, the Messiah comes, he will restore the genealogies by the Holy Spirit that shall rest upon him. "For," says Maimonides, "in the days of the Messiah, when his kingdom shall be established, all the Israelites shall be gathered together unto him; and all shall be classed in their genealogies by his mouth, through the Holy Spirit that shall rest upon him; as it is written, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.3">Mal 3:3</reference> : He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he shall purify the sons of Levi. First he will purify the Levites, and shall say: 'This man is a descendant from the priests; and this, of the stock of the Levites;' and he shall cast out those who are not of the stock of Israel; for behold it is said, <reference osisRef="Ezr.2.63">Ezr 2:63</reference> : And the Tirshatha said-they should not eat of the most holy things, till there stood up a priest with Urim and Thummim. Thus, by the Holy Spirit, the genealogies are to be revised." See Schoettgen. <div eID="gen51480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51481" type="x-p"/> Some learned men suppose that the apostle alludes here to the Aeons, among the Gnostics and Valentinians, of whom there were endless numbers to make up what was called their pleroma; or to the sephiroth, or splendours of the Cabalists. But it is certain that these heresies had not arrived to any formidable head in the apostle's time; and it has long been a doubt with me whether they even existed at that time: and I think it the most simple way, and most likely to be the intention of the apostle, to refer all to the Jewish genealogies, which he calls Jewish fables, <reference osisRef="Tit.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>, to which we know they were strongly and even conscientiously attached and which, at this time, it must have been extremely difficult to make out. <div eID="gen51481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51482" type="x-p"/> Instead of γενεαλογιαις, genealogies, some learned men have conjectured that the original word was κενολογιαις, empty words, vain speeches; but this conjecture is not supported by any MS. or version. <div eID="gen51482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51483" type="x-p"/> Which minister questions - They are the foundation of endless altercations and disputes; for, being uncertain and not consecutive, every person had a right to call them in question; as we may naturally suppose, from the state in which the genealogical tables of the Jews then were, that many chasms must be supplied in different lines, and consequently much must be done by conjecture. <div eID="gen51483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51484" type="x-p"/> Rather than godly edifying - Such discussions as these had no tendency to promote piety. Many, no doubt, employed much of that time in inquiring who were their ancestors, which they should have spent in obtaining that grace by which, being born from above, they might have become the sons and daughters of God Almighty. <div eID="gen51484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51485" type="x-p"/> Instead of οικοδομιαν Θεου, godly edifying, or the edification of God, οικονομιαν Θεου, the economy or dispensation of God, is the reading of almost every MS. in which this part of the epistle is extant, (for some MSS. are here mutilated), and of almost all the versions, and the chief of the Greek fathers. Of the genuineness of this reading scarcely a doubt can be formed; and though the old reading, which is supported by the Latin fathers and the Vulgate, gives a good sense, yet the connection and spirit of the place show that the latter must be the true reading. Griesbach has received this reading into the text. <div eID="gen51485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51486" type="x-p"/> What had Jewish genealogies to do with the Gospel? Men were not to be saved by virtue of the privileges or piety of their ancestors. The Jews depended much on this. We have Abraham to our father imposed silence on every check of conscience, and every godly reproof which they received for their profligacy and unbelief. In the dispensation of God, Faith in Christ Jesus was the only means and way of salvation. These endless and uncertain genealogies produced no faith; indeed they were intended as a substitute for it; for those who were intent on making out their genealogical descent paid little attention to faith in Christ. They ministered questions rather than that economy of God which is by faith. This dispensation, says the apostle, is by faith, οικονομιαν Θεου την εν πιστει· It was not by natural descent, nor by works, but by faith in Christ; therefore it was necessary that the people who were seeking salvation in any other way should be strictly informed that all their toil and labor would be vain.
entries.f7ec49fadec458562e1aea04fa2ff9861e7cc117: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51487" type="x-p"/> Now the end of the commandment is charity - These genealogical questions lead to strife and debate; and the dispensation of God leads to love both to God and man, through faith in Christ. These genealogical questions leave the heart under the influence of all its vile tempers and evil propensities; Faith in Jesus purifies the heart. No inquiry of this kind can add to any thing by which the guilt of sin can be taken away; but the Gospel proclaims pardon, through the blood of the Lamb, to every believing penitent. The end, aim, and design of God in giving this dispensation to the world is, that men may have an unfeigned faith, such as lays hold on Christ crucified, and produces a good conscience from a sense of the pardon received, and leads on to purity of heart; Love to God and man being the grand issue of the grace of Christ here below, and this fully preparing the soul for eternal glory. He whose soul is filled with love to God and man has a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.
