               <ns0:p n="1">1 PAul an Apostle of Jesus Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">One immediately sent by Jesus Christ, by his voice from Heaven, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.15. though not by his voice upon Earth (as those <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.)</ns0:note>, by the commandement of God our Saviour, and the Lord Jesus Christ: <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Through <ns0:hi>the will of God,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.1. not his <ns0:hi>permissive,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>preceptive</ns0:hi> will, and this is the same with his being called to be an Apostle, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1 1. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.1. by our <ns0:hi>Lord Iesus Christ,</ns0:hi> the Father not being excluded, but the Son on<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly being named, to whom the Mediatory Kingdom was com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitted.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Col. 1.27.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> our hope <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Our Hope,</ns0:hi> there is no more in the (Greek) that is, the <ns0:hi>ob<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ct of our Hope</ns0:hi>: as when 'tis said <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 31.53. that <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> sware by the <ns0:hi>fear of his Father Isaac,</ns0:hi> that is, by the Deity whom his Father feared. This glorious Eulogy belongs to our Saviour in whom there is a concurrence of all that is requisite to free us from destructive evils, and to make us everlastingly happy: for he is <ns0:hi>Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, and Redemption.</ns0:hi> Hence the <ns0:hi>Gentiles without Christ are said to be without hope, Eph.</ns0:hi> 2.12. And from hence tis evident that Jesus Christ is the Eternal God, for if he were only a man though in excellence above all others, he could not be our hope, <ns0:hi>for cursed is he that trusteth in man, Ier.</ns0:hi> 17.5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:530" />2 Unto <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Acts 16.1. 1 Thess. 2.2.</ns0:note> Timothy <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> own son in the faith: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 1.3. 1 Pet. 1.2.</ns0:note> Grace, mercy, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> peace from God our Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, and Jesus Christ our Lord.<ns0:note place="bottom">He dignifies <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> with the Title <ns0:hi>of his Son in the Faith</ns0:hi>: that is, being converted by him to Christianity, and begat to the Divine Life: and by stiling <ns0:hi>Timothy his own Son,</ns0:hi> he signifies his piety and vertue, that rendred him a worthy Son of such a Father, whom he imitated and honoured, and with whom he corresponded in a grateful obedient affection. Having thus de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />signed the person to whom he Writes, he expresses his ardent desires of his compleat felicity; which is included in <ns0:hi>Grace, Mercy,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Peace: by Grace</ns0:hi> he means the free favour and good will of God, with all the spiritual gifts that proceed from it, either requisite for Salvation, or the great work of the Evange<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lical Ministry: <ns0:hi>by Mercy,</ns0:hi> his compassionate tender Love, pardon<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, releiving, supporting and assisting us in our Christian course: by <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> he signifies, principally the Peace of God, that divine calm of Conscience, that tranquillity and rest of Soul which proceeds from the assurance that God is reconciled to us in Christ, and our freedom by the sanctifying Spirit, from the Tyranny of carnal lusts: <ns0:hi>This peace can never be to the wicked.</ns0:hi> And besides this principal peace, we may understand peace with man, that is a quiet state exempt from hatred and persecutions, that <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> might more comfortably and successfully perform the work of his Ministry. He prays for these blessings <ns0:hi>from God,</ns0:hi> who is the original Fountain of all good: and from <ns0:hi>Iesus Christ</ns0:hi> as the channel, by which all the gifts of God are conveyed to us. For without his mediation the Deity is as a sealed Fountain, no Grace would flow to us. He stiles God <ns0:hi>our Father,</ns0:hi> because he has adopted us in his Son, and in that quality he communicates his <ns0:hi>Grace, Mercy, and Peace</ns0:hi> to us: he stiles <ns0:hi>Christ our Lord,</ns0:hi> who hath supream power over us as well by the right of Creation as of Redemption.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi> was a great City in <ns0:hi>Asia</ns0:hi> the less, whither <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> came <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 19.1. where <ns0:hi>Demetrius</ns0:hi> raised a tumult against him; which the <ns0:hi>Town Clerk</ns0:hi> appeased as we read there. From thence he went into <ns0:hi>Macedonia. Acts</ns0:hi> 20.1, 2, 3. upon this his motion into <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> (as Divines judge) he left <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> at <ns0:hi>Ephesus.</ns0:hi> The end of leaving him at <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> was that <ns0:hi>he might charge some that they preached no other Doctrine,</ns0:hi> that is, none contrary to what he had preached, none contrary to the Doctrine of the Gospel, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 1.8, 9. what power was here committed to <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> is by some questioned, supposing (which is very probable) there were a greater number of Disciples then could meet in one Assembly, his power was more then Pastoral, for he had a po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer over the Teachers. Whether this power was <ns0:hi>extraordinary</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>ordinary,</ns0:hi> and what God intended ever to continue in the Church is the question. Those who make it to be such make it to be <ns0:hi>Episcopal,</ns0:hi> those that make it <ns0:hi>extraordinary,</ns0:hi> say it was the work of an <ns0:hi>Evangelist,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.4. That there was such an Officer in the Primitive Church appears from <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 21.8. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.11. That this was <ns0:hi>Timothy's</ns0:hi> work appears from 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.5. nor is it a new thing; but very common in the settlement of all new Governments, to authorize some special Commissioners and to give them an extraordinary power for a time till the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernment can be settled, and things brought into a fixed order. If we consider the words without prejudice, <ns0:hi>I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus,</ns0:hi> they seem to signifie that <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> was not the establisht Bishop of <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> for to what end should the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle desire a Bishop to reside in his own Diocess, which he could <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ot forsake without neglecting his duty, and the offence of God? This were a trait reflexion as if he were careless of his duty. And the word <ns0:hi>abide</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, does not necessarily import his constant residence there: for 'tis used to signifie continuance for some time only; as 'tis said of the Apostle, that remained <ns0:hi>many dares at Corinth, Acts</ns0:hi> 18.18. when his stay there was only for some Months. The intention of the Apostle seems to be that <ns0:hi>Timo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thy</ns0:hi> should continue for a while at <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> and not accompany him in his Voyage to <ns0:hi>Macedonia,</ns0:hi> as he was wont to do upon other occasions. And 'tis evident by the sacred History, that about six moneths after <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> was with the Apostle in <ns0:hi>Greece,</ns0:hi> that he went with him to <ns0:hi>Macedonia</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Troas,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Miletus, Acts</ns0:hi> 20.1, 4. where the Apostle sent for the Elders or Bishops of <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> to leave his last solemn charge with them. In short if <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> had been appointed the Bishop of <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> the Apostle would probably have given this Title of honour to him in the inscription of his Epistle. Upon the impartial considering of the whole matter, though the passion of Prelacy is so ingenious, as to discover so many mysteries and Myters in a few plain words, (<ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> was Bishop of that City, <ns0:hi>Metropolitan</ns0:hi> of the Province, and Primate of all <ns0:hi>Asia</ns0:hi>) yet 'tis most likely that <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> was left onely for some time with a kind of Apostolical power in the Church of <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi>; of which power this was one branch, authoritatively to command seducers not to teach another Doctrine, then what was taught by the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles who were divinely illuminated. A divine rule, and most worthy of perpetual observation by all in the office of the Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistry. And this sheweth the mighty proness of men as to deviate in their conversations from the right ways, so in their judgements from the truths of God, otherwise <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> had had no need to have left <ns0:hi>Timothy</ns0:hi> for that end, in this Church so newly planted.</ns0:note> `when I went into Macedonia <ns0:hi>g,</ns0:hi> that thou mightest charge some that they teach no other doctrine <ns0:hi>h.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Neither <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4.7.</ns0:note> give heed to fables <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Fables</ns0:hi> he probably meaneth the <ns0:hi>Iewish Fables, and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandments of men,</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>Titus</ns0:hi> 1.14. or more generally, all <ns0:hi>vain</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>idle speculations.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and end<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less genealogies, which minister questions rather then godly edifying <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whatsoever tendeth not to build men up in Godliness, (which is the end of Preaching.) The Jews had many unwritten Fables, about what God did before he made the World, &c. and many unwritten endless <ns0:hi>Genea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />logies,</ns0:hi> which were as so many Labyrinths, intricate without an issue out of them: and 'tis probable that some of them (con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verted to the Christian Faith) still busied their heads about, according to their Education, and the practice of the <ns0:hi>Iewish Doctors,</ns0:hi> and made the subject of their Sermons, and discourses to the assemblies of Christians; which is the thing the Apostle here declareth a corruption of the <ns0:hi>Ordinances of Preaching,</ns0:hi> and inveigheth against <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 6.4. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2.23. <ns0:hi>Titus</ns0:hi> 1.14. and 3.9. and willeth Preachers to avoid, and People to give no heed to them, as nothing tending to the building Christians up in holiness, which he here calleth <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the building up of God, either so <ns0:hi>objectively,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>efficiently,</ns0:hi> or by his command, because it is <ns0:hi>in God, viz.</ns0:hi> in the knowledge of God, and an increase in the Love of God, and other spiritual habits, or <ns0:hi>from God,</ns0:hi> being wrought by him, and serving for his honour and glory, or according to his Will.</ns0:note>, which is in faith <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For he tells us this edi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fying can be no otherwise then <ns0:hi>in Faith,</ns0:hi> Preaching the Doctrine of the Gospel, and imbracing that which is the <ns0:hi>Doctrine of Faith,</ns0:hi> a Doctrine of Divine Revelation, to which men must give their assent, because of the authority of God revealing it. So as no discourses which are not founded in a divine Revelation and to be proved from thence can possibly tend to any <ns0:hi>building of God,</ns0:hi> which <ns0:hi>cannot</ns0:hi> stand in the <ns0:hi>Wisdom of Men,</ns0:hi> but must stand <ns0:hi>in the po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer of God,</ns0:hi> from this Text we may observe the vanity and proneness of some persons even from the infancy of the Church, to make up what they call <ns0:hi>Sermons</ns0:hi> of discourses about <ns0:hi>Fables, Idle Questions,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Speculations,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Genealogies</ns0:hi> of which there is no end, the Teachers being able to bring the minds of hearers to no rest about them nor they tending to any good, and saving use, but meerly to shew mens <ns0:hi>Wit</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Parts,</ns0:hi> and we may also learn, that this is no religious <ns0:hi>Preaching</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Hearing,</ns0:hi> it being impossible men should be under any religious obligations to hear any but <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> that is, such as reveal the divine Will. For other discourses men in their seasons may hear them, or let them alone, and credit or not credit them as they see reason.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>so do.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Now the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 13.8, 10. Gal. 5.14,</ns0:note> end of the commandment is charity <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The word Translated <ns0:hi>Commandement</ns0:hi> here is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which rather signifies a particular charge given by superiors as to some thing, then a <ns0:hi>general Law, Acts</ns0:hi> 5.28. and 16.24. and so in this <ns0:hi>chapter ver.</ns0:hi> 18. which inclineth me to think that though the proposition be true of the whole Law of God, (<ns0:hi>for love is the fulfilling of the Law,</ns0:hi>) and more eminently of the divine Doctrine in the Gospel, for the end and perfection it aims at and produces is a pure ardent love of God, and of men for his sake, and of the Gospel, yet it is rather here to be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strained to the Commandement relating to <ns0:hi>Preaching,</ns0:hi> or dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />coursing the revealed Will of God relating to mens Salvation, the End of which is doubtless <ns0:hi>Charity,</ns0:hi> which ought to be <ns0:hi>finis operantis,</ns0:hi> the end of the workman, what he ought to intend and aim at; and is <ns0:hi>finis operis</ns0:hi> the effect of the work, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> the beget<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting in the Souls of people <ns0:hi>love to God and their Neighbour,</ns0:hi> neither of which can rationally be obtained, by Preachers telling people idle Stories, and filling their heads with idle questions and spe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culations.</ns0:note> out of a pure heart <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which love to God and men must proceed from a clean, and holy, and sincere heart.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> a good conscience <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And a good and holy life, when Conscience doth not sowrely reflect upon men, for presumptuous miscarriages. Which</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> faith unfeigned <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">must all be rooted in, and attended with a <ns0:hi>faith unfeigned</ns0:hi> rooted in it as Faith signifies a steady assent to Divine Revelation attended with it, as it signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fies, the Souls repose and rest upon Christ for the fulfilling of the promises annexed to him that beleives, and liveth up to such propositions. These are the noble the ends of whole Law of God, and particularly of the charge, or command God hath given Ministers as to Preaching, which can by no means be attained, by Teachers discoursing Fables and endless Genealogies to peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, nor by Peoples attendance to such discourses, for they can onely fill peoples heads with notions and unprofitable questions which serve to gender strife, and contention amongst people, instead of <ns0:hi>Love</ns0:hi> either to God or Men, and so to defile instead of purifying the Heart, and have no influence at all upon an Holy Life, all which can grow out of no root but an unfeigned Faith.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:530" />6 From which <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">From which things (for the article is plural <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.) From which Commandement, and from the end of which Commande<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, from which pure heart, good Conscience, and Faith unfeigned.</ns0:note>, some having <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>not aimed <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> swerved <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the word signifieth to <ns0:hi>wander from a scope or mark.</ns0:hi> Some men either propounding to themselves ends in their discourses to people different from the command con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning Preaching, and the true end of that, or at least wan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dring from that true end, they have turned aside. To do an action well, two things are necessary. 1. The propounding to our selves a right end. 2. A moving to it by due means and in right order, who so faileth in either of these, can no more do an action well, then he can shoot an Arrow well, that either eyeth no mark, or levelleth his Arrow quite besides it, the Preachers reflected on by the Apostle, either never considered the true end of Preaching, or never regarded it in their action; this made them turn aside from <ns0:hi>Theology</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Mataeology,</ns0:hi> from <ns0:hi>Preaching</ns0:hi> to</ns0:note>, have turned aside unto <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 6.4, 20.</ns0:note> vain jangling <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Vain Iangling,</ns0:hi> (so we translate it, but) the word signifieth <ns0:hi>foolish talking</ns0:hi> (so we translate the adjective, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 1.10.) and so the word properly signifieth, any kind of <ns0:hi>foolish</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>impertinent</ns0:hi> discourse either serving to no good end, or at least not that which the discourse pretendeth to. And indeed all discourses of Fables, and unprofitable, idle questions tending not to edifying, is no better then <ns0:hi>foolish talking.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Desiring to be teachers of the law <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. This Term lets us know that the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stle reflecteth upon some who were or had been <ns0:hi>Iewes,</ns0:hi> who ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther pressed the observance of the Law in order to justification, or spent their times in pressing the Traditions of the Elders, and constitutions of the Scribes, as <ns0:hi>sepimenta legis,</ns0:hi> Hedges (as they call'd them) to the Divine Law, though not of the Letter of it; upon which there arose a great many questions as insignificant as their Traditions themselves.</ns0:note>, under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which these vain Preachers spent their time in speaking to, neither understanding the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Law, nor the questions themselves started, and spoke unto, yet ambitious to be accounted <ns0:hi>Teachers of the Law.</ns0:hi> This vain desire of Reputation, as persons of excellent skil in the Land, was the cause of their erroneous idle Sermons: And their Ig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />norance is aggravated and inexcusable, in that they with pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sumptuous boldness assert the things of which they are ignorant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 But we know that the law <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Not that I speak against the Law of God, I know that it is holy, and spiritual, and just, and good, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 7.12, 14. It is good though not for Justification, yet for conviction, to convince men of sin, and as a Schoolmaster to lead men unto Christ, and to direct us in our walking with God; the equity and sanctity of its precepts are evident to the sincere and puri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied mind. And as the Law has an intrinsick goodness in its nature, so 'tis good to men when 'tis used for the end to which God, gave it.</ns0:note>, if it be used lawfully <ns0:hi>x.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 3.19. and 5.23.</ns0:note> Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>By the Law</ns0:hi> is to be understood the Moral Law, (though possibly not excluding the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> consisting in many Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinances) as 'tis armed with stings and terrours, to restrain re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bellious sinners; by the righteous man, one in whom a princi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of Divine Grace is planted, and from the knowledge and love of God, chooses the things that are pleasing to him, and is ardent and active to do his will. Now 'tis true, the holiness commanded in the Law, that consists in the love of God, and our Neighbour, obliges every reasonable creature indispensably and eternally, but as the Law was delivered in so terrible a man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner, as it has annext so many severe threatnings to the Trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gressours of it, 'tis evident, that 'tis directed to the wicked, who will only be compelled by fear from an outragious breaking of it. And this may be emphatically signified in the word here used <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, for it signifies to be <ns0:hi>laid,</ns0:hi> as well as to be made. The Law <ns0:hi>non objicitur</ns0:hi> is not laid against a righteous man. Thus we translate it, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 3.10. <ns0:hi>The Axe is laid to the root of the tree,</ns0:hi> there is some difference in the construction, here it is immedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ately joyn'd with the Dative case, there with an Accusative case, with the Preposition <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> betwixt the Verb and the Case, but that must be the sence. It is very probable, that these false Teachers had been terrifying the Christians with the Law, in opposition to whom the Apostle saith, the Law was not made for a righteous man, as to its condemning office, it was never intended against a righteous man, but against men that com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitted and lived in gross sin and wickedness. These sinners are first mentioned in general terms, then the Apostle proceed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth to a more particular enumeration of them, whether in them (as some think) the Apostle hath respect to the several precepts of the Decalogue, I cannot determine.</ns0:note>, but for the lawless <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>Law<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less</ns0:hi> he meaneth persons living without any respect to the Lawes of God or Men.</ns0:note> and disobedient <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By the <ns0:hi>disobedient</ns0:hi> he meaneth such as will live in subjection to no Government.</ns0:note>, for the ungodly <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The word by us Tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slated <ns0:hi>ungodly,</ns0:hi> signifieth, such as live without any Religion, ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving no regard to the Worship of God, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

               <ns0:p n="11">11 According to the glorious gospel of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap, 6.15.</ns0:note> the blessed God <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 2.4.</ns0:note> which was committed to my trust.<ns0:note place="bottom">Here the Apostle specifies the sound Doctrine of which he spake; that 'tis contained in the Gospel the perfect rule of righ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />teousness which he stiles <ns0:hi>the glorious Gospel of the blessed God,</ns0:hi> it being a Doctrine revealed from Heaven, wherein the concurrence and command of the Divine Attributes, Wisdom, Power, Mercy, and Justice doth most clearly shine to the Glory of God, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.6. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.6, 12. and he gives the Title <ns0:hi>of blessed to God,</ns0:hi> thereby to signifie his transcendent goodness, in that being in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />finitely happy in the possession of his own excellencies, without any possible advantage and profit from any Creature, yet he was pleased to give his Son to be our ransom, and with him Grace and Glory to us.                <ns0:p n="12">12 And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, put<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting me into the ministry.<ns0:note place="bottom">Here St. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> expresses his most humble and solemn thanks to Christ for his rich favour in calling him to the High Office of an Apostle: for by <ns0:hi>the ministry,</ns0:hi> that is to be understood, and 'tis so called by way of excellence, it being the most glorious and Divine Ministry that ever was establisht in the Church: and he ascribes to our Saviour the praise of all that he performed in the faithful discharge of it. He saith, <ns0:hi>Christ enabled me,</ns0:hi> that is, endowed him with Fidelity, Zeal, Courage, and all other qualifications requisite for that honourable and difficult Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stry, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.5, 6. The end of that Sacred Ministry was to inlighten and reform the World from superstition, and that vicious and vain conversation that was so pleasing to carnal men, to abolish those corrupt customs that had taken such deep root, and to plant the truth that comes from above, and to pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lish a holy Law so opposite to corrupt nature. This work was opposed by the craft and cruelty, the artifice and violence of the powers of darkness in conjunction with the perverted World. And the Glory of the Apostles resisting such Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies is entirely due to Christ. He adds as a motive of his thank<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness, that Jesus Christ <ns0:hi>counted him faithful,</ns0:hi> which is an evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent proof that he intends that he made him faithful. His faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness was not the cause or motive, but the fruit and effect of the Grace of God in calling him to the ministry. This he expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly declares 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.25. <ns0:hi>Having obtained mercy to be faithful.</ns0:hi> If our Saviour had only discovered his fidelity, without bestowing that Grace upon him, there had not been a reason of such af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fectionate thanksgiving: for that alwaies supposes some favour and benefit received.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 15.9.</ns0:note> Who was before a blasphemer <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The kindness of God putting me into so noble a service was the greater and more thank-worthy, because before that time I was a <ns0:hi>blasphemer,</ns0:hi> one who spake of Christ reproachfully, (for that blasphemy signifieth) <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was a zealous man in the Jew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ish Religion, his blasphemy therefore only respected the Second person in the Trinity, which the Jews owned not. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pelled others to <ns0:hi>blaspheme Acts</ns0:hi> 26.11.</ns0:note>, and a persecutor <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Of his persecution, see <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 8.3. he entred houses, <ns0:hi>haled Men and Women to prison, he breathed threatnings and slaughter against the Disciples of the Lord, Acts</ns0:hi> 9.2. he persecuted Christianity even to Death, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 22.4, 5.</ns0:note>, and injurious <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Thus he was <ns0:hi>injurious,</ns0:hi> for in other things he was as <ns0:hi>to the law blameless, Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.6. bred up a <ns0:hi>Pharise<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

Act. 3.17.</ns0:note> I did <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> ignorantly <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Because he did it <ns0:hi>ignorantly</ns0:hi> we cannot reasonably think that ignorance of the Divine Law (once published) should excuse any transgressor of it, we see men will not allow it as to their Laws, after promulgation, so that although <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> persecuted Christians <ns0:hi>ignorantly,</ns0:hi> yet he stood in need of <ns0:hi>Mercy. Ignorance</ns0:hi> excuseth not <ns0:hi>a toto,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>a tanto,</ns0:hi> not in whole, but in part, and makes the sinners sin not to be so exceeding sinful, especially where it is not vincible. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s ignorance here mentioned was <ns0:hi>vincible,</ns0:hi> he lived in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> where the Gospel had been preached some years, before he persecuted the Professors; he might have heard the Sermons, and seen the miracles preached, and wrought by Christ and the Apostles, but he was bred a <ns0:hi>Pharisee,</ns0:hi> and under the prejudices of that Sect which were implacable Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies to Christ, this kept him in <ns0:hi>ignorance,</ns0:hi> Christ allows some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing for the prejudices of mens Education.</ns0:note>, in unbe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lief <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He did what he did also while he was in a state of <ns0:hi>unbelief.</ns0:hi> He believed one true and living God, (all the Jews did so) and worshipped him according to the Jewish manner, yet stiles himself an unbelie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver. Every man is an <ns0:hi>unbeliever</ns0:hi> (in a Gospel sense) that re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceiveth not Jesus Christ as the Son of God, and his Saviour; though he believes there is one God, <ns0:hi>&c.
